title: @burkov
summary:
This paper reformulates long-context language modeling as a continual learning problem, where a standard Transformer with a sliding-window attention mechanism is allowed to keep learning during inference via next-token prediction on the provided context, effectively compressing the context into its own parameters.
The method replaces the standard full self-attention mechanism, which has computational cost that grows quadratically with context length, with a much more efficient sliding-window attention mechanism, whose cost grows only linearly. However, sliding-window attention alone performs worse on long-context tasks. By allowing the model to update a subset of its weights on the fly using the incoming context, it compensates for this performance drop, effectively regaining modeling capability without reverting to the slower full attention.

title: @burkov
summary:
When asking Claude to implement a serious change involving modifying too many files, it can die before it completes. A trick is to ask it to split the work into stages and put the stages in order of importance, from foundational changes to features.
Once it lists the stages, ask it to implement Stage 1 only and provide updated files. Integrate these files and ask it to proceed to Stage 2, etc.
This way, even if it dies in the middle, you can copy the initial list of stages and start a new session with Claude by asking it to verify whether the stages that were supposed to be implemented are complete and, if yes, proceed to the next unimplemented stage.

title: @burkov
summary:
In transformers, self-attention layers process sequences without built-in notions of order, so positional embeddings—vectors added to token representations to encode their positions—are used to provide that information.
Rotary positional embeddings, or RoPE, a common type that applies rotations to queries and keys in attention, turn out to accelerate training by giving gradient descent a helpful starting bias that makes convergence happen faster, as shown through analysis of attention patterns and gradients.
At the same time, keeping RoPE after training restricts the model from handling sequences longer than its original context length without further adjustments, because the rotations become unfamiliar at new positions.
Removing these embeddings post-training and running a short recalibration at the original length lets the model adapt while preserving its short-context abilities, enabling it to work on much longer inputs immediately, with experiments across model scales up to billions of parameters demonstrating better retrieval and perplexity than standard scaling techniques.

Claude is great at coding. Like really, really good, compared to using a regular LLM like Gemini.
There's only one issue with it. Because it never sees the full code of the app but uses grep search for relevant code snippets, it's myopic.
If grep returns a fragment of code similar to the bug description, it often doesn't look further and fixes an irrelevant part of the app or answers a question based on these fragments found by grep.
So, as the codebase grows, it becomes important for the user to know the codebase. Otherwise, Claude will reinvent the bicycle over and over again, creating duplicate implementations for the same functionalities in different places in the app.
This issue is probably fixable with additional finetuning, but right now this is how it works.

title: @burkov
summary:
The Hundred-Page Machine Learning book by Andriy Burkov is widely considered a valuable and highly effective resource for gaining a solid, concise overview of the entire machine learning field. It is praised by industry experts and practitioners for its clarity and practical focus, serving well as both an introduction and a quick reference guide.
Here's why readers love It:
**Concise and Comprehensive:** The primary strength is its ability to cover a vast range of essential topics, from fundamental algorithms (linear regression, decision trees) to advanced areas like deep learning, clustering, and recommendation systems, in a remarkably short format (around 150 pages).
**Practical Focus:** The book prioritizes techniques that are proven to have significant practical value in the real world, reflecting the author's extensive industry experience.
**Right Level of Detail:** It includes necessary mathematical equations without getting bogged down in theoretical abstractions, striking a good balance for those with a basic college-level math background.
**Strong Supplementary Materials:** It comes with a companion wiki, accessible via QR codes in the book, which provides additional Q&A, code snippets, further reading, and other resources that are actively updated by the author.
**Endorsed by Experts:** The book has received strong endorsements from prominent figures in the AI/ML community, including Peter Norvig (Google) and Aurélien Géron (author of another ML bestseller).
In summary, The Hundred-Page Machine Learning Book is an excellent resource if you want a structured, high-level overview and a reliable reference guide for the core concepts of machine learning. It is best used as a starting point that you can revisit often, supplemented with more specialized resources and hands-on practice to build deeper expertise.

title: @burkov
summary:
Ok, when I see myself accused of bullshitting, I fight back.
Me saying that you should stop reading AI-generated code isn't just some clickbait or hot take you are used to on this platform.
When I'm saying something, it's based on knowledge, hands-on experience, and thinking, a lot of thinking.
Why should we all stop reading AI-generated code? It's because of how the machine generating it was built.
Take Claude in particular. This isn't a vanilla LLM. It's a system that was finetuned end-to-end to maximize reward using a reinforcement learning algorithm.
The reward is assigned by a script. The script breaks working code, asks Claude to fix it, and Claude can use tools such as grep and python to get this reward.
Claude doesn't care about the beauty of the code, there's no reward for this. Claude cares about getting a high reward from this script that broke the code. Therefore it needs to come up with working code.
The script that decides whether code works runs code, sees the output, compares it to the expected output, and returns reward. There's no beauty of code in its logic, because it's a script. If the output is the same as expected, the script returns 1. If it isn't, the script returns 0. The script will optionally subtract from the reward the number of tokens used by Claude to come to the solution.
What does that mean for us humans? Claude will generate whatever gets it this reward, and it will try to get it by using the fewest tokens possible.
Therefore, if it gets it a higher reward, Claude will generate an ugly mess. As long as this mess is short and it works, Claude is happy.
So, yes, stop reading AI-generated code.
Currently, Anthropic might have some part of the reward that honors some notion of readability. But they only do that because there are still coders who aren't ready to move on.
But the industry will move on; it already is moving on, and Anthropic will remove this "readability" reward component, because having it hurts performance.
Why? Because if you are something of a scientist yourself, you know that you cannot optimize multiple objectives at the same time, so you either maximize the chance for code to run, or you minimize the number of used tokens, or you maximize the readability.
Which one of the three do you think the industry really cares about?

title: @burkov
summary:
I spent today working in parallel with Kimi K2.5 in its official CLI and also in Claude Code CLI.
Some say here that they don't see any difference between the two. Indeed, visually both work the same way by using grep to find relevant fragments of code in the large codebase and by applying surgical patches to files.
The difference, however, is major. First of all, Claude is so much faster. I'm tired of waiting for Kimi to finish the fix.
But the speed wouldn't be a major obstacle for me if not for this fundamental difference: Claude was trained to write expendable test scripts in Python and run them to see the console log. This gives it a huge source of information Kimi doesn't have: how the code actually runs and what output it produces.
Kimi is like Gemini: it can pretend via thinking that it executed some code, but it's a hallucinated simulation, not the actual code execution.
So until someone trains their LLM to write and run expendable scripts, nothing compares to Claude Code.

title: @burkov
summary:
I didn't want to comment on OpenClaw. Usually, when there's so much noise in the media, it's some ordinary stuff just hyped well.
So I took time to learn how it works thanks to open source.
I was right. OpenClaw is 2% of ordinary stuff and 98% of hype.
To put it very shortly, in case you were wondering, there are two things in it:
1. You can chat with an LLM via a text messenger. Not anything new.
2. The LLM can use tools that run on your computer. Not anything new either.
Most of the "magic" mentioned in the media is about its ability to use the browser.
But it's not *its* ability. It's Playwright's ability.
Playwright is a library made by Microsoft which allows you to programmatically run a browser. It uses a built-in vision model made by Microsoft that converts the browser's screen into a textual description for LLMs.
Again, Microsoft has built Playwright exactly for what OpenClaw is using it.
So, OpenClaw's typical workflow:
1. The user types in a text messenger "Buy me a flashlight on Amazon."
2. OpenClaw blindly dispatches this message to an LLM which has access to some tools, including Playwright.
3. The LLM, trained not by OpenClaw folks, decides that Playwright is the right tool (of course it is) and Amazon is the URL to navigate to.
4. Playwright, built not by OpenClaw folks, runs the browser, which navigates to Amazon, and returns the textual description of what Amazon's home page looks like.
5. OpenClaw blindly returns to the LLM this textual description.
6. The LLM (again without any help from OpenClaw) decides that one should type "flashlight" into the search field and press Search, so it calls the Playwright tool with the search parameters.
7. OpenClaw calls Playwright because the LLM told it to and types "flashlight" and then presses Search (it's all part of what Playwright does out of the box).
...
In the end of this LLM-controlled scenario, the order is submitted. OpenClaw just listened to what the LLM told it to do via tool calls.
I tried hard, and I haven't found anything else worth mentioning in the source code. There's also a part that keeps "memories" about past conversations, but it's all basic stuff. These memories are stored in text files and grep (controlled by LLMs trained to use grep, and trained not by OpenClaw folks) is used to search in them.
It's a nice hobby project, just like Cursor or Perplexity are nice hobby projects, but there's nothing there to look for, except for the hype and 2% of unoriginal plumbing code.

title: @burkov
summary:
"The Hundred-Page Language Models Book: Hands-On with PyTorch" by Andriy Burkov is widely regarded as a strong resource for anyone looking to grasp the fundamentals and intricacies of language models, particularly large language models (LLMs). Published in 2025 as a follow-up to Burkov's highly acclaimed "The Hundred-Page Machine Learning Book," it maintains the series' signature style: distilling complex topics into a compact, accessible format without sacrificing depth or rigor.
### Content and Scope
The book spans roughly 100 pages, focusing on a progressive journey from foundational concepts in machine learning and language modeling to advanced topics in modern LLMs. It starts with basics like count-based methods, neural networks, and tokenization, then builds toward Transformer architectures, pre-training, finetuning, alignment, and practical applications such as instruction finetuning and prompt engineering. Burkov emphasizes hands-on learning, incorporating working Python code examples using PyTorch, along with mathematical explanations presented intuitively through diagrams and clear derivations. This makes it particularly valuable for developers, data scientists, and ML engineers who want to implement concepts rather than just theorize.
Key topics include:
- The evolution of language models, from simple predictive objectives (e.g., next-token prediction) to scalable generative behaviors.
- Differences in tokenization strategies (e.g., characters vs. subwords) and their impact on model performance.
- Real-world techniques like semantic search, reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF), and working with LLMs in production.
College-level math is recommended for full appreciation, but the book avoids overwhelming readers by using examples and visuals to clarify equations. It's not a exhaustive encyclopedia—it's designed as a "hundred-page" primer, so it prioritizes breadth and clarity over exhaustive detail on niche subtopics.
### Strengths Based on Reception
Reviews and endorsements praise the book for its clarity and efficiency, especially in an era where LLM literature can feel bloated or overly academic. One reviewer notes that it explains complex ideas—like transformers and finetuning—"in a way that is rigorous but also accessible," making it a "compact yet rigorous entry point" between a survey paper and a full textbook. This echoes the success of Burkov's prior work, which was lauded as "the book I wish I had when I started learning machine learning" for its reference-like quality—something to revisit repeatedly rather than read once.
Professionals highlight its practical bent: the inclusion of code snippets and diagrams helps bridge theory and application, turning abstract concepts into actionable insights. For beginners navigating LLMs, it's positioned as an excellent starting point, while experienced practitioners appreciate it as a refresher or quick reference on evolving techniques. Endorsements from tech leaders and its coverage in AI communities (e.g., KDnuggets, LinkedIn discussions) underscore its relevance in a fast-moving field.
Compared to denser texts like "Deep Learning" by Goodfellow et al. or specialized LLM papers, Burkov's book stands out for its conciseness—compressing what could fill multiple volumes into a digestible read that can be completed in a day or two, yet retained as a go-to guide.
### Who Should Read It?
This book is ideal if you're an aspiring AI engineer, a developer curious about LLMs, or a professional seeking a streamlined update on language model advancements. If your goal is to quickly build intuition and hands-on skills without wading through hundreds of pages, it's a smart choice. For those already deep in the field, it serves as a solid reference or teaching tool.
In summary, the book is arguably excellent for its purpose. Its blend of theory, math, code, and brevity makes it a standout in the crowded LLM space, earning praise for demystifying a complex topic without dumbing it down.

title: @burkov
summary:
Most neural networks see the input data as a matrix or a vector, like pixels in rows and columns or words in a sequence.
A lot of real-world data is better described as a graph: a set of nodes connected by edges, like social networks, power grids, or molecules.
Graph neural networks try to process this kind of data, and the most common approach before this paper (GCNs) treated every neighbor of a node as equally important when aggregating information. This ICLR 2018 paper, published by Bengio's team and since then garnered more than 18,000 citations, introduces Graph Attention Networks (GATs), which borrow the idea of attention in language models to let each node learn which of its neighbors matter more for a given task.
The attention weights are computed using a small shared neural network that looks at pairs of connected nodes, so the model doesn't need to know the full graph structure ahead of time and can generalize to entirely new graphs it's never seen during training.
It's an exemplary AI research paper. The architecture is simple enough to describe in a few equations, runs efficiently in parallel, and at the time matched or beat everything else on standard benchmarks.

These benchmarks 😞 This is how you break them:
1. Ask your most capable model to read a public task A and generate a similar task and then solve it. Given that the solution is verifiable, you get a collection of task-solutions similar to public task A but not copying it.
2. Then you do the same for public task B, etc.
3. Once you have this collection of synthetic tasks, you finetune your most capable model to solve these tasks so it becomes better. Better for this benchmark and nothing else.
Rinse. Repeat.

title: @burkov
summary:
Previously, Google Search dominated in:
1. Index freshness
2. Speed of search
3. Accuracy of search
The search accuracy here is the chance of putting the right result among the top 3 search results.
LLMs made the second and third advantage irrelevant. As long as the right result is in the top 20, answering the user's question will be quick enough. And the competitors are already doing that.
Competing only on index freshness isn't a viable strategy because it's not a huge moat and the competitors are quickly catching up.
So, not only is Google's index getting increasingly polluted by the AI slop, which is unfixable, it can no longer compete in anything the competitors don't know how to do right.

A math professor noticed his kitchen sink at home was leaking.
He called a plumber.
The plumber came the next day, tightened a couple of nuts, and the sink worked perfectly again. The professor was delighted. But when, a minute later, the plumber handed him the bill, he was shocked.
“This is a third of my monthly salary!”
“Yeah, I get it…” said the plumber. “Why don’t you come work for our company as a plumber? You’ll make three times more than you do as a professor. Just remember: when you apply, say you only finished seventh grade. They don’t like hiring educated people.”
So the professor got a job as a plumber, and his life really did improve. All he had to do was tighten a nut here and there every so often, and his salary was much higher.
One day, the management of the plumbing company decided that every plumber had to attend evening classes to finish eighth grade. So our professor had to go too.
By chance, the very first class was math.
The evening school teacher, wanting to check what the students knew, asked for the formula for the area of a circle.
They called the professor up to the board, and he suddenly realized he’d forgotten it. He started frantically reasoning it out, covering the board with integrals, differentials, and all sorts of fancy formulas to re-derive the result. In the end, he got:
S = –π r²
He didn’t like the minus sign, so he started again.
Again he got a minus. No matter what he did, it kept coming out negative.
He cast a panicked look at the class, and all the plumbers were whispering:
“Swap the limits of integration!”

summary:
Vanilla Transformer-based LLMs are slow at generating text because, at each step, they need to load from memory a set of cached values (called "keys" and "values") that help the model decide what to pay attention to from earlier in the conversation.
A previous technique called multi-query attention (MQA) shrinks this cache by sharing a single set of keys and values across all the model's parallel attention computations (called "heads"), which speeds things up a lot but hurts output quality.
This landmark paper, published by Google researchers, introduces grouped-query attention (GQA), which splits the attention heads into a few groups, each sharing their own set of keys and values — so you get most of the speed benefit without losing much quality.
On top of that, the authors show you don't need to train a model with GQA from scratch: you can take an existing vanilla model that was trained the normal way, average together its key and value weights into the grouped structure, and then do a short round of additional training using only about 5% of the original training cost.
The results show that this converted model nearly matches the quality of the original while running almost as fast as the most aggressive compression.
It's one of those papers where a relatively simple idea had an outsized practical impact — it changed how nearly all major open-weight LLMs are built within months of publication, and it remains the default attention configuration for production models today.

title: @burkov
summary:
When you train a neural network on a new task using examples (through supervised finetuning), it tends to forget what it already knew — a well-known problem called catastrophic forgetting.
The standard fix in reinforcement learning is to have the model learn from its own outputs rather than from a fixed dataset (this is called "on-policy" learning), but that requires a reward function telling the model how good its outputs are, which is often hard to define.
This recent MIT paper finds a way around that constraint: it uses the same model twice — once with a demonstration stuffed into its input as context (the 'teacher'), and once without (the 'student') — then has the student generate text, and updates the student's weights so that its token probability distributions get closer to the teacher's token probability distributions at each position in that generated text.
The trick works because LLMs can already adapt their behavior when shown an example in context, so the teacher is essentially a better version of the model that stays close to the original, making the learning signal gentle enough to avoid wrecking existing capabilities.
Across multiple experiments, this approach lets a single model sequentially learn three different skills while keeping all of them, where standard supervised training destroys earlier skills as soon as it moves to the next one.
The math also turns out to be equivalent to a form of reinforcement learning with an implicit reward, which gives the method a clean theoretical grounding beyond just "it works empirically."

title: @burkov
summary:
LLMs process text from left to right — each token can only look back at what came before it, never forward. This means that when you write a long prompt with context at the beginning and a question at the end, the model answers the question having "seen" the context, but the context tokens were generated without any awareness of what question was coming. This asymmetry is a basic structural property of how these models work.
The paper asks what happens if you just send the prompt twice in a row, so that every part of the input gets a second pass where it can attend to every other part. The answer is that accuracy goes up across seven different benchmarks and seven different models (from the Gemini, ChatGPT, Claude, and DeepSeek series of LLMs), with no increase in the length of the model's output and no meaningful increase in response time — because processing the input is done in parallel by the hardware anyway.
There are no new losses to compute, no finetuning, no clever prompt engineering beyond the repetition itself.
The gap between this technique and doing nothing is sometimes small, sometimes large (one model went from 21% to 97% on a task involving finding a name in a list). If you are thinking about how to get better results from these models without paying for longer outputs or slower responses, that's a fairly concrete and low-effort finding.

title: @burkov
summary:
Attention in transformers works by having each token look at every other token in the context — which gets very expensive as contexts grow longer, and modern use cases like document search or step-by-step reasoning often involve tens or hundreds of thousands of tokens.
This paper from Microsoft Research starts from two observations:
1. After the softmax operation, most of those attention weights are already near zero anyway (only a small fraction of tokens actually matter for any given computation);
2. Which tokens matter tends to stay consistent across nearby layers of the network.
From these two facts, the authors build a method that does the full, expensive attention calculation only in a few selected layers, then reuses those results in the layers in between — skipping most of the work without asking the model to retrain or change its weights at all.
An important feature of the proposed approach is the engineering around it: how to automatically pick which layers to treat as reference points for any given model, how to handle the fact that different attention heads within the same layer may care about different tokens, and how to make this run efficiently on actual hardware.
The reported speedups — around 4× for the generation phase (on top of what GQA already provides; see this paper to learn about GQA — come with benchmarks showing the outputs remain close to what a full attention model would produce, including on hard math reasoning problems where earlier methods of this kind had struggled.

I once needed money, so I joined an offshore software outsourcing company in Ukraine as a shit-coder for $100/month.
I had just finished university and had no experience as a coder. In my first week at work, they gave me a bug to fix. The application was (it's funny that the application still exists and looks as shitty as I remember it 25 years ago).
The application had a huge codebase in ColdFusion; it was written in India by folks who asked slightly more than $100/month for their work, and it looked and worked accordingly.
As I said, I had zero experience with debugging such a large application, so I asked my manager's manager for help.
He looked at the error message that mentioned the file where it failed, then went to the directory with this file, searched for the variable that caused the issue, then saw in what file this variable was mentioned. Then he mounted like that about three levels, found the file where it was created and what values it could contain at the creation time, compared the observed value and the expected one, and figured out what was wrong at the time the variable was created.
I was so impressed that one could start in some unknown place and, by doing variable tracing to the source through files using simple string match, come to the place where it all becomes clear.
With time, I realized that this is a pattern that a software developer uses most of the time when debugging: string search -> file search -> string search -> file search.
This is why good developers keep their codebase neat: this simplifies the manual search and understanding of what to search for next.
The LLMs have learned this simple but powerful pattern the moment they were given access to grep and glob with one difference: they don't need the code to look neat; they don't analyze the text the same way humans do. So, for an LLM, it doesn't matter whether you, a human, think that its code is maintainable *by you* or not. It's maintainable by using the attention-glob-grep combo, and that's enough.
Saying that you don't accept AI-generated code because you cannot maintain it by hand is the same as saying that you don’t accept mass-produced electronics because you can’t manually fix or replace every component.

summary:
For most of the 2010s, convolutional neural networks (ConvNets) — networks that process images by sliding small filters across them to detect patterns — were the dominant architecture for computer vision. Then transformers arrived.
Transformers, originally designed for text, process input by letting every element attend to every other element simultaneously, and when adapted for images they started outperforming ConvNets on benchmark after benchmark. The general consensus became that transformers were just better, and ConvNets were the old way.
This paper's authors decided to test whether that conclusion was actually justified, or whether ConvNets had simply fallen behind in terms of training recipes and design choices rather than fundamental capability.
They took a standard ResNet and systematically updated it — one change at a time — borrowing design decisions from transformers: things like which activation function to use, which type of normalization to apply, and how to reshape the internal dimensions of each processing block.
Each change was small and interpretable, and the paper tracks the accuracy at every step so you can see exactly what each decision contributes.
The final result is a pure ConvNet that matches or beats transformer-based models of equivalent size on image classification, object detection, and segmentation, by being up to 49% faster.

title: @burkov
summary:
There's a common assumption in AI right now that if one language model can do a task reasonably well, having several of them collaborate — splitting up the work, checking each other's outputs, debating answers — should do it better.
This paper puts that assumption under a controlled experiment across 180 configurations and finds that the reality is messier and more interesting: multi-agent setups improved performance by up to 81% on some tasks and made things worse by up to 70% on others, with the difference coming down to whether the task can be broken into parallel pieces or whether each step depends on the previous one.
In a financial analysis, one agent can look at regulatory filings while another reads market news and a third examines earnings data — none of them need to wait for the others.
In a Minecraft crafting puzzle, on the other hand, each action changes the inventory that the next action depends on, so the steps have to happen in order and splitting them across agents just adds overhead without any benefit.
The paper fits an equation that predicts which architecture will work best for a new task 87% of the time.
For anyone building or thinking about building systems where multiple AI models work together, this replaces a lot of hand-waving with something concrete.

title: @burkov
summary:
In a Generative Adversarial Network, a piece of technology that has shown for the first time that a machine can be made capable of generating images indistinguishable from man-made ones, a generator network tries to produce realistic data while a discriminator tries to distinguish generated samples from real ones.
For this to work, you need a way to measure how close the generated distribution is to the real one — and the standard measures turn out to have a serious flaw: when the two distributions don't overlap much, which is almost always true early in training, they go flat and stop providing useful gradient signals.
This paper works through exactly why that happens, shows that the Wasserstein distance — which measures how much "effort" it would take to reshape one distribution into the other — stays well-behaved even in that situation, and builds a practical GAN training algorithm around it that is more stable, less sensitive to architectural choices, and for the first time produces a loss number that actually correlates with output quality.
A great example of scientific research where an existing science invented earlier is applied to a new science invented much later, and it all fits.

Diffusion language models represent a fundamental reimagining of how machines generate text — moving away from the autoregressive, left-to-right token prediction that has dominated the field, toward an iterative denoising process borrowed from continuous diffusion in vision.

title: @burkov
summary:
Google just published TurboQuant a model compression technique that can quantize the transformer's key-value cache to just 3 bits without requiring training or finetuning and causing any compromise in model accuracy, all while achieving a faster runtime than the original LLMs.
As you might already know, LLMs store intermediate computations in something called a key-value cache — essentially a running memory of what the model has processed so far — and this cache grows linearly with the length of the input, eating up GPU memory fast.
The standard fix is quantization: representing each number with fewer bits (say 4 instead of 16), which shrinks the cache but introduces error. The problem is that most quantization methods need to store extra correction constants for every small block of data, and those constants themselves take up 1–2 bits per number, which is a lot when you're trying to get down to 3 or 4 bits total.
TurboQuant gets around this by combining two ideas: PolarQuant, which converts vectors into a coordinate system (radius and angle instead of x/y/z) where the data distribution is predictable enough, and QJL, a 1-bit scheme that needs only a single sign bit per number with no extra correction constants stored alongside — so the 1 bit is the entire cost.
PolarQuant does the heavy lifting as the first compression stage, and QJL is then applied to the small residual error PolarQuant leaves behind — not to eliminate it, but to remove its systematic bias so it doesn't consistently skew attention scores.
The papers report compressing the cache to 3 bits **with no measurable accuracy loss** on standard benchmarks and up to 8x speedup on attention computation, and the methods come with actual theoretical guarantees.
All three papers are available on @chapterpal to read with an AI tutor. Suggested reading order:
QJL first, then PolarQuant then TurboQuant. The first two are independent building blocks, and TurboQuant combines them.
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HESlqOhbYAAEIHI.jpg

title: @burkov
summary:
When you want a large language model to get better at a specific task—like solving math problems or navigating websites—the standard approach is to finetune it: you adjust the model's internal parameters using training data and gradient descent, which is expensive, requires lots of data, and often makes the model worse at everything else.
Instead of changing the model's parameters, this paper proposes to run the model on a small set of problems multiple times, compare the successful and failed attempts, and use the model itself to write down natural-language "lessons learned"—things like "when solving geometry problems, always check that your solution falls within the valid region."
These lessons get iteratively refined across a few rounds and then get pasted into the prompt at inference time.
The method is modeled after GRPO, a reinforcement learning algorithm where you generate a group of outputs, score them, and use the relative quality differences to improve the model—except here the "improvement" happens in the prompt text rather than in the weights.
The paper shows that doing this with just 100 training examples and about $18 worth of API calls on a large frozen model (DeepSeek-V3.1-Terminus, 671 billion parameters) outperforms smaller models that were finetuned with thousands of examples at costs exceeding $10,000.
The results hold across both math reasoning and web search tasks, and unlike finetuned models that degrade when moved to a different domain, swapping in a different set of learned experiences lets the same frozen model perform well in multiple domains simultaneously.

Quoting @burkov
Just like Python won the race among programming languages not because it was the fastest to run but because it was the fastest to code, LLM-based software development will surpass coding from scratch because it offers the quickest path from 0% to 90% completion.
Software development companies will start hiring coders who can demonstrate in interviews that they master AI-assisted coding tools like Copilot or Cursor.
Selling access to frontier LLMs has become a race to the bottom, with pay-per-token prices plummeting from $30 per million tokens to $0.1 in just a year. Anyone can now access LLM-based coding virtually free of charge. It's naive to think that software engineering organizations or departments won’t leverage this tool.
Claims that LLMs can’t write reliable code are immature. Most junior and mid-level coders can’t write reliable code either. This is why software engineering has, over decades, equipped itself with automated and semi-automated tools to ensure that code is production-ready.
There are already LLMs fine-tuned specifically for coding. Companies are investing hundreds of millions of dollars to improve LLM coding skills because it's currently the only use case where, if done right, you can charge $10 or even $100 per million tokens from corporate clients.
If you build a reputation as the go-to business for that—like Google did for search—you’ll be able to charge much more than $0.1 per million tokens because better coding directly translates into ROI. Better math or logic doesn’t.

clean_title: Uniqueness-aware reinforcement learning for diverse problem-solving in LLMs
summary:
"Rewarding the Rare: Uniqueness-Aware RL for Creative Problem Solving in LLMs"
When you train a language model with reinforcement learning to solve math or science problems, it tends to find one approach that works and then stick with it — generating the same kind of solution over and over, just with minor wording differences.
This matters because in practice, users often sample multiple answers from a model and hope that at least one is correct (a metric called pass@k), so having diverse strategies is important.
Most existing fixes try to encourage variety at the level of individual word choices (token-level entropy), but two solutions can use completely different words while following the exact same reasoning strategy — like solving a quadratic equation with the quadratic formula twice, just showing different intermediate steps.
This 2026 paper, published by a collaboration of scientists from MIT, Yale, and several others, takes a different route: during training, it uses a separate language model to look at all the candidate solutions for a given problem, group them by their actual high-level strategy (e.g., "factoring" vs. "quadratic formula" vs. "graphical method"), and then gives a bigger training signal to correct solutions that used rarer strategies.
The mechanism is simple — just multiply the standard advantage (the signal that tells the model which outputs to reinforce) by a weight inversely proportional to how many other solutions used the same approach.
Across math, physics, and medical reasoning benchmarks, this keeps the model exploring different solution paths as training progresses, instead of collapsing onto a single dominant one, and it does so without hurting accuracy.

The paper presents a novel method where a separate language model evaluates candidate solutions, groups them by high-level strategies, and provides stronger training signals for less common approaches. This technique encourages exploration of varied solution paths during training without sacrificing accuracy, as demonstrated across benchmarks in math, physics, and medical reasoning.

title: @burkov
clean_title: Generative Modeling via Drifting: A new approach to single-step image generation
summary:
Most generative models that produce high-quality images — diffusion models and flow-based models — work by running the neural network many times in sequence during generation: you start from noise and take dozens or hundreds of small steps to gradually clean it up into an image.
Each step requires a full pass through the network, which is slow and expensive. There have been many attempts to compress this into a single step, but they typically start from the multi-step framework and try to approximate or distill it.
This paper takes a different route. It notices that training itself is already an iterative process (gradient descent updates the network over and over), so you can let that iteration do the distributional work instead of piling it on at generation time.
The authors define a "drifting field" — a vector that tells each generated sample how to move based on its relationship to real data (which pulls it closer) and to other generated samples (which push it away).
When the generated distribution matches the real one, this field becomes zero, so the training has a natural stopping condition.
The network is just a single-pass mapping from noise to data, no sequential denoising needed.
With this setup, the authors get a single-step generator that scores 1.54 FID on ImageNet 256×256 — better than all previous single-step methods and competitive with multi-step diffusion models that run the network hundreds of times.
The author also show that the approach works for robot control policies.
It's a nice paper. The framework is clean and the math is accessible, especially with an AI tutor.

Most generative models that produce high-quality images, like diffusion and flow-based models, require multiple passes through the neural network during generation, which is slow and costly. This paper proposes a novel approach by leveraging the iterative nature of training itself, allowing the model to use gradient descent updates to perform the distributional work instead of relying on multi-step generation.

The authors introduce a 'drifting field' that guides each generated sample based on its relationship to real data and other generated samples. When the generated distribution aligns with the real one, the field becomes zero, providing a natural stopping condition for training. This results in a single-pass generator that achieves a score of 1.54 FID on ImageNet 256×256, outperforming previous single-step methods and competing with multi-step diffusion models. The approach is also applicable to robot control policies, showcasing its versatility.

clean_title: Improving reinforcement learning for language models with separate reward normalization
summary:
When training a language model with reinforcement learning, you typically score each generated response with a reward and nudge the model toward responses that score above average within a small batch of attempts at the same prompt.
This averaging-and-rescaling step is what GRPO, the current default method, does. Modern training setups increasingly use several rewards at once — say, one for correctness and one for keeping the answer short — and the standard practice is to add these rewards together before doing the averaging.
The authors of this paper point out that this addition step throws away information, because once summed and normalized within the small batch, distinct combinations collapse onto the same number. They show this collapse worsens as you add more rewards or generate more attempts per prompt, and they trace concrete training failures to it — models that stop improving partway through, or never learn the output format at all.
Their fix is to normalize each reward separately before adding, which is a small change to existing code but recovers the lost distinctions and produces measurably better results across tool use, math, and coding tasks.

PDF:
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HFQ9o92aoAAhVaf.jpg
clean_summary:
When training a language model with reinforcement learning, responses are typically scored with a reward to guide the model toward better outputs. The current default method, GRPO, averages and rescales these rewards, but this approach can lose important information when multiple rewards are combined before averaging.

The authors highlight that this loss of information leads to training failures, such as models that stop improving or fail to learn the correct output format. Their proposed solution is to normalize each reward separately before summing them, which recovers lost distinctions and results in better performance across various tasks, including tool use, math, and coding.

title: @burkov
clean_title: New method for accelerating diffusion models without approximation
summary:
Diffusion models are slow because generating one image takes hundreds of sequential passes through a neural network. People have spent enormous effort trying to speed this up, usually by training a second "student" network to imitate the slow process in fewer steps, with mixed results.
This paper shows a way to train such a model so that all those hundreds of steps provably collapse into a single pass, with no approximation and no student-teacher distillation.
The same construction also gives you, for free, the ability to take a real image and find the noise that would generate it (something diffusion models normally can't do cleanly), and to build networks that are exactly idempotent—meaning running them twice does the same thing as running them once.
For instance, finding the noise that generates a given real image is what lets you edit that image with a diffusion model. If you want to take a photo of a face and change the hairstyle, or take a painting and restyle it, you first need to locate where that image "lives" in the model's input space. Without that, diffusion models can only generate from scratch—they can't take something you already have and modify it. Current methods for doing this inversion are approximate, sometimes fail to reconstruct the original faithfully, and add computational cost on top of already slow generation. A clean, exact inversion would make image editing with these models work the way people intuitively expect it to.

title: @burkov
clean_title: Evolution strategies outperform reinforcement learning for LLM fine-tuning
summary:
For the past few years, the standard recipe for finetuning LLMs on tasks like math reasoning has been reinforcement learning (RL): you let the model generate answers, score them, and use the scores to nudge the model's parameters via gradients.
RL has known weaknesses here—it struggles when rewards only arrive at the end of long answers, it often "hacks" the reward by finding degenerate shortcuts, and two runs with identical settings can end up with very different final performance.
This paper shows that an old and much simpler family of methods, called evolution strategies, works well on models with billions of parameters, which most researchers had assumed was impossible.
The method is straightforward: take the model, make thirty copies with small random noise added to every parameter, score each copy on the task, then shift the original parameters slightly toward the copies that scored higher. No gradients, no backpropagation, no value networks, no penalty terms to tune.
Using this approach, the authors finetune models from the Qwen and Llama families on a symbolic arithmetic puzzle, several math benchmarks, and Sudoku, and match or beat welltuned RL baselines while keeping the same hyperparameters across every experiment.
Read with an AI tutor:
PDF:
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HFXmZ7tXYAEyzHU.jpg
clean_summary:
For the past few years, the standard recipe for fine-tuning large language models (LLMs) on tasks like math reasoning has been reinforcement learning (RL). However, RL has known weaknesses, such as struggling with delayed rewards and producing inconsistent results.

This paper demonstrates that evolution strategies, a simpler family of methods, can effectively fine-tune models with billions of parameters, which was previously thought impossible. The method involves creating multiple copies of the model with slight random noise, scoring each copy, and adjusting the original parameters toward those that performed better. This approach successfully fine-tunes models from the Qwen and Llama families on various math tasks, matching or exceeding the performance of well-tuned RL baselines while maintaining consistent hyperparameters across experiments.

Using evolution strategies simplifies the fine-tuning process by eliminating the need for gradients, backpropagation, and complex tuning parameters.

title: @burkov
clean_title: ICLR Test of Time Award for 'Auto-Encoding Variational Bayes'
summary:
An ICLR Test of Time Award: "Auto-Encoding Variational Bayes"
This is the paper that introduced the variational autoencoder.
Before it, training generative models with continuous hidden variables ran into a wall: computing the exact probability a model assigns to an image requires integrating over every possible hidden representation that could have produced it, and for anything involving a neural network that integral has no closed form.
Existing workarounds either needed slow per-datapoint sampling loops or imposed restrictive assumptions on the model. Kingma and Welling show that if you let a second neural network guess the hidden representation from the input, and you sample that representation in a particular way — drawing random noise from a fixed distribution and then transforming it with the network's output, rather than sampling from the network's output directly — the whole system becomes differentiable end to end and trainable with ordinary gradient descent.
That one move, now called the reparameterization trick, is the piece worth seeing derived from scratch, because it shows up throughout modern generative modeling and in places you would not expect, including the noise schedules of diffusion models and several reinforcement learning methods.
The paper is short, the math is followed step by step rather than hidden in appendices, and reading it gives you a clear view of how an idea from Bayesian statistics turned into a practical tool for training neural networks on images.
A must-read.
Published on @ChapterPal thanks to a kind permission from Prof Kingma.
Read with a friendly AI tutor:
PDF:
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HFaEzqKXwAAm2dH.png
clean_summary:
An ICLR Test of Time Award goes to the paper "Auto-Encoding Variational Bayes," which introduced the variational autoencoder. Before this work, training generative models with continuous hidden variables faced significant challenges due to the need to compute exact probabilities by integrating over all possible hidden representations, a task that lacks a closed form in neural networks.

Kingma and Welling demonstrated that by allowing a second neural network to infer the hidden representation from the input and by sampling that representation using a fixed distribution transformed by the network's output, the entire system becomes differentiable and trainable via gradient descent. This reparameterization trick is fundamental in modern generative modeling, appearing in various applications, including diffusion models and reinforcement learning methods. The paper is concise, with clear mathematical derivations, making it essential reading for understanding how Bayesian statistics can be applied to neural network training.

title: @burkov
clean_title: Why LLMs cannot understand the world regardless of size
summary:
Why LLMs cannot understand the world no matter their size?
You will walk a street and look at passersby faces. Then I'll ask you what the ratio of happy to unhappy faces was, and you will tell me, approximately.
An LLM will observe these passersby faces with you, then you train it on these faces, and then you will ask it the same question. It will fail to return a consistent result.
LLMs can only answer questions when the answers have been given to them, and they can interpolate from multiple partial answers.
LLMs cannot know how many people's faces they had in the training set and therefore cannot calculate this simple statistic.
Learning from lifelong continuous experiences, and not from aggregated sources of useful statistics, is what makes animals, including humans, so good at understanding the world.
clean_summary:
Why can't large language models (LLMs) understand the world, no matter how large they are? Imagine walking down a street and observing the faces of passersby. If I ask you the ratio of happy to unhappy faces, you can provide an approximate answer. An LLM, however, would observe the same faces, be trained on them, and still fail to give a consistent result when asked the same question.

LLMs can only answer questions based on the information they have been given and can interpolate from multiple partial answers. They lack the ability to know how many faces were in their training set, preventing them from calculating simple statistics like these. This highlights that learning from continuous, lifelong experiences—rather than from aggregated statistics—is what enables animals, including humans, to understand the world effectively.

title: @burkov
clean_title: VOID: Training a video diffusion model for object removal with counterfactual reasoning
summary:
Most work on video object removal treats the problem as inpainting: fill in the pixels where the object used to be.
That framing ignores the fact that objects in real scenes do things—they hold up other objects, cast shadows, block what would otherwise move. Remove the hand and the ball it was holding should fall.
VOID is an attempt to train a video diffusion model to handle this counterfactual reasoning, using paired training data where one video contains an object and the other shows what the scene would have looked like without it.
The paired data comes from two sources with known physics: a rigid-body simulator and a motion-capture dataset of people interacting with objects, which together give around 6,400 examples.
The authors show how far a diffusion model can be pushed toward physical plausibility when the training signal explicitly encodes cause and effect rather than just appearance.
Read with an AI tutor:
PDF:
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HF0CkB0aQAEwiqa.jpg
clean_summary:
Most work on video object removal treats the problem as inpainting, filling in the pixels where the object used to be. This approach overlooks the dynamics of real scenes, where objects interact with their environment, such as casting shadows or supporting other objects. VOID aims to train a video diffusion model to incorporate this counterfactual reasoning by using paired training data: one video with an object and another showing the scene without it.

The paired data is sourced from a rigid-body simulator and a motion-capture dataset, providing around 6,400 examples. The findings demonstrate how a diffusion model can be pushed toward physical plausibility when the training signal encodes cause and effect rather than just appearance.

title: @burkov
clean_title: Using experience replay to improve reinforcement learning for language models
summary:
In reinforcement learning for language models, the model generates candidate answers, each one receives a score, and gradient updates push the model toward higher-scoring outputs.
Most current pipelines discard each generated answer after a single gradient step, on the grounds that an answer produced by an older version of the model is too stale to be useful.
In this paper, the @AIatMeta and @nyuniversity researchers question this. Generating those answers consumes more than 80% of the compute budget in state-of-the-art training runs, and they show that keeping answers in a storage structure—a replay buffer—and sampling from it repeatedly cuts that cost by roughly 40% without hurting final accuracy, and sometimes improves it, since the extra diversity of older samples seems to prevent the model from overfitting to its own recent outputs.
Beyond the measurements, the paper derives explicit formulas relating three quantities: how stale a sample can be before reusing it hurts more than it helps, how many times each sample should be reused, and how expensive generation is relative to a gradient step.
The framing shifts attention from how much each gradient step improves the model to how much improvement per unit of compute, which is what determines whether a training run is affordable.

📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HGJn1iPaQAESHa-.jpg

title: @burkov
clean_title: Native Sparse Attention: A new approach to transformer efficiency
summary:
Attention is the mechanism inside a transformer where each token in a sequence computes a relevance score against every other token, then produces a weighted combination of their values. The cost grows with the square of the sequence length, which becomes the main bottleneck for long inputs. Sparse attention is any method that skips most of those pairwise comparisons—letting each token look at only a small subset of the others—on the theory that most attention scores are near zero anyway.
The standard approach takes a transformer that was trained with full attention and applies sparsity only at inference time, pruning computations on a model that never learned to operate under that constraint.
In this Best Paper Award ACL 2025 paper Yuan et al. train the sparse pattern from scratch, with gradients flowing through the block selection mechanism during pretraining itself. Their 27B-parameter model matches or beats a dense baseline across general benchmarks, long-context tasks, and chain-of-thought reasoning, with measured speedups of 9x on forward pass, 6x on backward, and 11.6x on decoding at 64k context on A100 hardware.
The paper also walks through concretely why prior sparse methods failed to deliver practical speedups: clustering-based selection causes load imbalance in mixture-of-experts systems, per-head selection conflicts with the shared key-value cache in grouped-query attention (where multiple query heads share one set of keys and values for memory efficiency), and token-level selection breaks the contiguous memory access that FlashAttention relies on for throughput.
Section 6.1 shows loss curves from two alternative designs the authors tried and abandoned before arriving at the published architecture, and the appendix places two reasoning traces side by side on the same competition math problem—the sparse model reaches the correct answer in 2,275 thinking tokens while the dense baseline takes 9,392 and arrives at the wrong one.
Read with an AI tutor:
PDF:
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HGNlqKVbQAANbFM.jpg
clean_summary:
Attention is the mechanism inside a transformer that computes relevance scores between tokens, leading to a cost that grows with the square of the sequence length, which becomes a bottleneck for long inputs. Sparse attention methods aim to reduce these computations by allowing each token to focus on a small subset of others.

In the Best Paper Award-winning ACL 2025 paper by Yuan et al., the authors train a 27B-parameter model with a natively trainable sparse attention mechanism from scratch, achieving performance that matches or exceeds dense baselines across various benchmarks. The model demonstrates significant speedups—9x on forward pass, 6x on backward, and 11.6x on decoding at 64k context on A100 hardware. The paper also discusses the limitations of prior sparse methods and presents loss curves from alternative designs that were ultimately abandoned, highlighting the effectiveness of their approach.

clean_title: LeWorldModel solves representation collapse in generative AI
summary:
Read to understand with @ChapterPal:
PDF:
Quoting @HowToAI_
Yann LeCun was right the entire time. And generative AI might be a dead end.
For the last three years, the entire industry has been obsessed with building bigger LLMs. Trillions of parameters. Billions in compute.
The theory was simple: if you make the model big enough, it will eventually understand how the world works.
Yann LeCun said that was stupid.
He argued that generative AI is fundamentally inefficient.
When an AI predicts the next word, or generates the next pixel, it wastes massive amounts of compute on surface-level details.
It memorizes patterns instead of learning the actual physics of reality.
He proposed a different path: JEPA (Joint-Embedding Predictive Architecture).
Instead of forcing the AI to paint the world pixel by pixel, JEPA forces it to predict abstract concepts. It predicts what happens next in a compressed "thought space."
But for years, JEPA had a fatal flaw.
It suffered from "representation collapse."
Because the AI was allowed to simplify reality, it would cheat. It would simplify everything so much that a dog, a car, and a human all looked identical.
It learned nothing.
To fix it, engineers had to use insanely complex hacks, frozen encoders, and massive compute overheads.
Until today.
Researchers just dropped a paper called "LeWorldModel" (LeWM).
They completely solved the collapse problem.
They replaced the complex engineering hacks with a single, elegant mathematical regularizer.
It forces the AI's internal "thoughts" into a perfect Gaussian distribution.
The AI can no longer cheat. It is forced to understand the physical structure of reality to make its predictions.
The results completely rewrite the economics of AI.
LeWM didn't need a massive, centralized supercomputer.
It has just 15 million parameters.
It trains on a single, standard GPU in a few hours.
Yet it plans 48x faster than massive foundation world models. It intrinsically understands physics. It instantly detects impossible events.
We spent billions trying to force massive server farms to memorize the internet.
Now, a tiny model running locally on a single graphics card is actually learning how the real world works.
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HGXB-TTb0AASwdD.jpg

For years, JEPA suffered from representation collapse, where the AI oversimplified reality. Researchers have now introduced LeWorldModel (LeWM), which solves this issue with a simple mathematical regularizer that enforces a Gaussian distribution on the AI's internal thoughts. This allows LeWM to understand the physical structure of reality, enabling it to plan 48 times faster than larger models while only using 15 million parameters and training on a single GPU in a few hours. This approach fundamentally changes the economics of AI, allowing smaller models to learn how the real world works effectively.

clean_title: Direct Preference Optimization: A new approach to aligning language models
summary:
NeurIPS 2023 Outstanding Main Track Runner-Up:
Direct Preference Optimization: Your Language Model is Secretly a Reward Model
The training of LLMs often requires an alignment stage to ensure the model's behavior matches human preferences for safety and helpfulness. Traditionally, this was achieved through Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF), a complex three-phase process that involves training a separate reward model to score outputs and then using reinforcement learning to update the language model based on those scores.
This 2023 paper marked a significant shift in the field by introducing Direct Preference Optimization (DPO), which mathematically demonstrates that the language model can be finetuned on human preferences directly without needing a separate reward model or the unstable reinforcement learning loop.
By treating alignment as a simple classification task—similar to the basic binary cross-entropy loss used in supervised learning—DPO provides a stable and computationally lightweight alternative that matches or exceeds the performance of traditional RLHF.
This streamlined approach has since become dominant in modern AI development, offering a theoretically grounded and practical path for aligning increasingly large models with human values.

title: @burkov
clean_title: The impact of public research on private AI development
summary:
No matter how hard you, as a closed private company, try to build the strongest AI model, and no matter how much you spend on achieving your goal, public research scientists will discover your science virtually weeks after your technology is seen.
And given that you don't have any vendor lock-in, clients will go where it's cheaper. And given that your competitors will get the same tech for free from public research, it will be cheaper at your competitors.
Just look at the robotic dogs. Boston Dynamics invested hundreds of millions into their robotic dog. Now, Chinese companies sell them for the price of a scooter because they just saw how it had to be done. And this is robotics, where you can file and enforce a patent.
clean_summary:
No matter how hard a closed private company tries to build the strongest AI model, and no matter how much it spends, public research scientists will discover the underlying science virtually weeks after the technology is seen. Without vendor lock-in, clients will choose cheaper options, and competitors will access the same technology for free from public research, making it cheaper for them.

For example, Boston Dynamics invested hundreds of millions into their robotic dog, but now Chinese companies sell similar models for the price of a scooter because they learned how to do it. This situation highlights the challenges in robotics, where patents can be filed and enforced.

title: @burkov
clean_title: Understanding the limitations of LLM-based agents in general-purpose problem solving
summary:
If you don't understand this, you will not understand why LLM-based agents are irreparably failing for a general-purpose problem solving.
An agent (by the way it was the topic of my PhD 20 years ago) to be useful, must be rational. Being rational means to always prefer an outcome that results in the maximal expected utility to its master/user.
Let’s say an agent has two actions they can execute in an environment: a_1 and a_2.
If the agent can predict that a_1 gives its user an expected utility of 10, and a_2 gives an expected utility of -100, then a rational agent must choose a_1 even if choosing a_2 seems like a better option when explained in words. The numbers 10 and -100 can be obtained by summing the products of all possible outcomes for each action and their likelihoods.
Now here is the problem with LLM-based agents.
The LLM is not optimizing expected utility in the environment. It is optimizing the next token, conditioned on a prompt, a context window, and a training distribution full of examples of what helpful answers are supposed to look like.
Those are not the same objective.
So when we wrap an LLM in a loop and call it an “agent,” we have not created a rational decision-maker. We have created a text generator that can imitate the surface form of deliberation.
It may say things like:
“I should compare the expected outcomes.”
“The best action is probably a_1.”
“I will now execute the optimal plan.”
But the internal mechanism is not selecting actions by maximizing the user’s expected utility. It is generating a continuation that is statistically appropriate given the prompt and prior context.
This distinction matters enormously.
For narrow tasks, the imitation can be good enough. If the environment is constrained, the actions are simple, and the success criteria are close to patterns seen in training, the system can appear agentic.
But for general-purpose problem solving, the gap becomes fatal.
A rational agent needs stable preferences, calibrated beliefs, causal models of the world, the ability to evaluate consequences, and the discipline to choose the action with maximal expected utility even when that action is boring, non-linguistic, or unlike the examples in its training data.
An LLM-based agent has none of that by default.
It has fluency. It has pattern completion. It has a remarkable ability to compress and recombine human text. But fluency is not rationality, and a plausible plan is not an expected-utility calculation.
This is why these systems so often fail in strange, brittle, and irreparable ways when given open-ended responsibility.
They are not failing because the prompts are insufficiently clever.
They are failing because we are asking a simulator of rational agency to be a rational agent.
clean_summary:
If you don't understand this, you will not understand why LLM-based agents are irreparably failing for general-purpose problem solving. An agent must be rational, meaning it should always prefer outcomes that maximize expected utility for its user. For example, if an agent has two actions, a_1 and a_2, and can predict that a_1 yields an expected utility of 10 while a_2 yields -100, it must choose a_1, even if a_2 seems better in words.

The issue with LLM-based agents is that they do not optimize expected utility; instead, they optimize the next token based on a prompt and context. This means that when we call an LLM an “agent,” we have not created a rational decision-maker but a text generator that mimics deliberation. While it may articulate plans and comparisons, it does not select actions to maximize expected utility.

This distinction is crucial. For narrow tasks, the imitation might suffice, but for general-purpose problem solving, the lack of rational decision-making becomes fatal. A rational agent requires stable preferences, calibrated beliefs, causal models, and the ability to evaluate consequences, none of which LLM-based agents possess by default. They may be fluent and capable of pattern completion, but fluency does not equate to rationality, leading to failures when given open-ended responsibilities.

8. AI Engineering (Chip Huyen, 2025): Covers LLMs in production, most relevant for building with Claude/GPT.
9. LLM Engineer's Handbook (Iusztin & Labonne, 2024): Comprehensive guide on RAG, fine-tuning, agents, and evaluations, written by engineers who shipped LLM products.

title: @burkov
clean_title: Integrated Gradients: Axiomatic Attribution for Neural Networks
summary:
Attribution—figuring out which input features are responsible for a neural network's output, such as which pixels in an image led to its classification—is a problem with no obvious right answer, and the field had accumulated several competing methods that often disagreed on the same input.
Rather than judging methods by how convincing their visualizations look, the authors of this ICML 2017 paper write down two properties any reasonable attribution method should have, then demonstrate that most existing techniques (raw gradients, DeepLift, LRP, guided backpropagation, deconvolution) violate at least one.
The first property says that a feature whose change actually moves the prediction should not receive zero credit; the second says that two networks computing the same function should produce identical attributions regardless of how they are internally wired.
Their proposed method, Integrated Gradients, averages the gradient along a straight line from a chosen reference input (a black image, for vision models) to the actual input, and this small construction satisfies both properties while requiring no modifications to the model—just repeated calls to the standard gradient operator used in backpropagation.
They also link their straight-line choice to a result from cost-sharing in game theory, which singles it out among possible paths as the unique one that treats symmetric features identically.
Both the method and the framing have aged well: Integrated Gradients still appears in interpretability toolkits nearly a decade later, and the broader move of using a few explicit axioms to cut through a debate that empirical comparison alone could not settle is a useful template for other machine learning problems where ground truth is unclear.

title: @burkov
clean_title: The need for embedding-based context storage in LLMs
summary:
The fact that the context of LLMs, especially in the agentic setting, is still stored as raw text instead of a continuously updated embedding tensor surprises me.
People invent crazy tricks to paraphrase or regex-replace the long context into a shorter text, or to use images to contain the context's text and then OCR these images.
A scientific solution must be embedding-based, and the neural network must learn end-to-end to embed the context of any length by learning a gating mechanism that decides what the embedding tensor must absorb and what it should ignore.
Text must only be needed in the output because code is text and the user can read text. The model must think and remember in embeddings.

title: @burkov
clean_title: Estimating parameters in closed source LLMs using factual questions
clean_summary:
In this article, the authors apply a methodology to estimate the number of parameters in frontier closed source LLMs. They build a dataset of 1,400 factual questions spanning seven tiers of obscurity, deliberately selecting facts that cannot be derived by reasoning or compressed away by smarter architectures. They evaluate 89 open-weight models with known parameter counts (ranging from 135M to 1.6T parameters across 19 vendors) on this benchmark, fit a log-linear regression between IKP accuracy and log(parameters), and then plug closed-source frontier models into that calibration curve to back out their parameter counts.

The intuition is based on an information-theoretic lower bound: storing F facts requires at least F divided by the bits per parameter in weights, meaning what a model knows lower-bounds how many parameters it has.

summary:
Mamba 3 is a non-Transformer LM architecture.
Unlike attention, which maintains a growing KV cache that scales with sequence length, Mamba-3 compresses all past context into a fixed-size state of a fixed dimensionality​.
Each decode step therefore takes constant time regardless of how long the sequence is, making total decoding cost linear in sequence length.
The performance on the 1.5B parameter scale is comparable to Transformer with much faster inference with context sizes above 16k (see the table below).

title: @burkov
clean_title: Investigating Recursive Language Models and their alternatives
summary:
Language models have a fixed limit on how much text they can process at once — their context window — and even within that limit, performance degrades on information sitting far from the question.
One recent approach, called Recursive Language Models or RLMs, has the model treat a long input as a variable in a sandbox programming environment and write small programs that query and slice it, sometimes calling itself as a subroutine on the resulting pieces.
This paper from Apple investigates whether the recursion is what makes RLMs work. The authors compare against an alternative they call SRLM, which keeps the programmatic environment but drops the recursive self-queries.
SRLM matches or exceeds RLM by up to 22 points across the benchmarks tested, even when allowed no recursion at all, suggesting that the gains attributed to recursion mostly came from externalizing the context into a programming environment in the first place.

clean_title: Google DeepMind's approach to interleaving RLHF phases
summary:
Reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF)—the technique for getting large language models to follow instructions—usually operates in two separate phases: collect a large set of human judgments comparing pairs of model responses, then train a reward model (a network that scores responses) and use those scores to push the language model toward higher-rated outputs.
Google DeepMind researchers instead interleave the two, updating both models as each new comparison arrives, and pick which response pairs to send to humans based on which choice would be most informative.
Informativeness rests on a small ensemble of networks attached to the reward model, which produces a spread of reward predictions instead of a single number; pairs where ensemble members disagree most about the winner are the ones routed to humans.
They report needing roughly 10x fewer human labels than standard offline RLHF at the 20K-comparison scale, and project a 1000x reduction at one million comparisons.

PDF:
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HH0RtsmWQAgWKUf.jpg
clean_summary:
Reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF) typically operates in two phases: collecting human judgments on model responses and then training a reward model to score those responses. Google DeepMind researchers propose an alternative method that interleaves these phases, updating both models with each new comparison and selecting response pairs for human evaluation based on informativeness.

Informativeness is determined by an ensemble of networks attached to the reward model, which provides a range of reward predictions. Pairs with the most disagreement among ensemble members are prioritized for human labeling. This approach reportedly requires about 10 times fewer human labels than standard offline RLHF at the 20K-comparison scale, with projections suggesting a 1000 times reduction at one million comparisons.

title: @burkov
clean_title: The impact of copyright on academic publishing and accessibility
summary:
When I started my PhD 20 years ago, most conferences required that I give up my copyright on the paper if I wanted to get published in the conference proceedings.
Conferences themselves often didn't get the copyright either. The copyright went to greedy commercial publishers like Springer and Elsevier, along with non-profit professional societies like IEEE and ACM that behaved similarly.
These bastards added little value relative to what they charged. They just took papers the production of which were paid by the public money, put them online behind a paywall, and charged $30-$50 per download.
So, if you are a scientist working in a public university, you would have to pay $30-$50 to those monopolies to download a paper of your colleague from another public university while the latter would pay the same amount to download yours.
Of course, doing research like that would become extremely expensive, so these monopolies signed unlimited download agreements with each university in the world (there are tens of thousands of them) for something like $1M/year per publisher. So, public money was paid again, now to let scientists read one another's works.
Luckily, computer science people realized with time that the public is being robbed. Several prominent researchers stood up against this situation and said that they will no longer publish their works in conferences demanding giving up the copyright.
The most respected AI conferences like NIPS, ICML, and ICLR now only license the right to publish the paper, while the authors retain the copyright.
AI journals like JMLR and JAIR went further, and all papers published in these journals are licensed under the CC-BY Creative Commons license, which allows unrestricted use by anyone for anything.
But greedy bastards still keep the copyright on research that happened before the 2020s, and thus, the universities still pay them millions every year.
Today, anyone can publish their work on arXiv, and many scientists think that this makes their work accessible to anyone and allows their research to freely spread across the globe, but this is not exactly the case.
The default arXiv license is that arXiv has a non-exclusive right to host the paper. If the scientists haven't changed the license setting when submitting their paper to arXiv, this means that only arXiv has the right to host this paper or its part. No one else, not even a scientific news outlet, can use even a small fragment from the paper in their publication.
This significantly limits the reach of such a paper. If magazines or scientific news websites cannot use the paper, then only those who know about it will read it.
If you are a young or not so young scientist, please do consider setting the CC-BY, the CC-BY-SA, or the CC-ZERO license (like this paper when submitting to arXiv. Otherwise, only if you are from a big lab, published in a top-tier conference, or have a large network, will your paper become known and hopefully used to advance science.
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HH1UNvHXsAoI0fu.png
