This led to a situation where researchers at public universities had to pay to access each other's work, prompting universities to sign costly unlimited download agreements with publishers. Fortunately, the computer science community recognized this issue, and many top AI conferences now allow authors to retain copyright. Journals like JMLR and JAIR have adopted Creative Commons licenses for unrestricted use.

However, older research still falls under the control of these publishers, costing universities millions annually. While arXiv allows for paper publication, the default license limits distribution, making it essential for authors to consider setting a more open license like CC-BY when submitting their work to maximize accessibility and impact.

This paper is now on @ChapterPal:
Quoting @hardmaru
The human brain🧠 is incredibly efficient because it only activates the specific neurons needed for a thought. Modern LLMs naturally try to do this too (> 95% of neurons in feedforward layers stay silent for any given word), but our hardware punishes them for it.
One of the most frustrating paradoxes in deep learning: making a model do less math often makes it run slower. Why? Because unstructured sparsity introduces irregular memory access, and GPUs are built for predictable, dense blocks of math.
We teamed up with @NVIDIA to try to fix this hardware mismatch. Instead of forcing the GPU to adapt to the sparsity, we built a "Hybrid" format that reshapes the sparsity to fit the GPU. Our sparsity format (TwELL) dynamically routes the 99% of highly sparse tokens through a fast path, and uses a dense backup matrix as a safety valve for the rare, heavy tokens.
Through TwELL and a new set of custom CUDA kernels for both LLM inference and training, we translated theoretical sparsity into actual wall-clock speedups: >20% faster training and inference on H100 GPUs, while also cutting energy consumption and memory requirements.

title: @burkov
clean_title: The lineage of agentic AI traced back to Google Research's ICLR 2023 paper
summary:
Most of what's now called "agentic AI" — language models that browse, click, search, and take actions in an environment — traces its lineage back to this ICLR 2023 paper from Google Research.
Rather than have a language model either reason silently and produce an answer (chain-of-thought prompting, where the model writes out its thinking before the final response) or just emit actions in an environment, the authors proposed to interleave the two.
The model writes a thought, takes an action, sees the result, writes another thought, continues. The prompts are a handful of human-written examples of this pattern, no finetuning required.
On Wikipedia question answering, letting the model look facts up rather than recall them drops the hallucination rate from 56% in pure chain-of-thought to roughly zero.
On a household-simulation game and an online shopping benchmark, prompting with one or two example trajectories beat imitation-learning and reinforcement-learning baselines trained on tens of thousands of demonstrations, by 34 and 10 percentage points respectively.
Three and a half years on, the thought–action–observation loop is still the basic structure every tool-using assistant runs.
Basically, Google invented everything modern AI is: self-attention and the agentic loop. The only question is why it took OpenAI for Google to actually start building products with it.

clean_title: The West's decline in building infrastructure and its impact on AI
summary:
The West has become incapable of building. This is not an exaggeration. When was the last time a bridge was built around where you live? Or a new power plant? Or a new railway? Or a new highway?
The West has a hard time building even regular houses so that they are affordable for regular workers.
China has no such issues.
The West has conserved itself, made incapable of change. And it's human ability to adapt to changing conditions that made us the dominant species.
The West lost the very quality it needs to survive.
Quoting @r0ck3t23
Elon Musk just revealed what’s actually holding AI back.
It’s not chips. Not models. Not data.
It’s concrete.
Someone asked him the obvious question. Why not just build private power plants next to data centers? Bypass the grid entirely.
His answer was four words.
Musk: “The power plant makers.”
There aren’t enough of them.
You can design the best chip on earth. Train a frontier model. Raise $10 billion for a hyperscale data center.
None of it matters if you can’t power it.
Musk: “You can drill down a level further.”
GPUs need power. Power needs turbines. Turbines need factories. Factories need permits. Permits need a government that hasn’t paralyzed itself.
Every link in the chain is physical. And every one of them is breaking.
We can train a frontier model in weeks. We can’t permit a power plant in under five years.
The country that invented the assembly line now needs 40 agencies to approve a gas turbine.
China doesn’t have this problem. They don’t run 7-year environmental reviews on infrastructure they need tomorrow. They break ground while America requests approval to break ground.
The AI race won’t be decided by whoever writes the best algorithm.
It’ll be decided by whoever can still build in the physical world.
We spent 30 years getting faster in software and slower in steel. Outsourcing manufacturing. Hollowing out supply chains. Treating builders like liabilities instead of assets.
Now the bill is due.
Every breakthrough in AI is gated by atoms. Steel. Concrete. Turbines that take years to manufacture and decades to approve.
The smartest code on earth is worthless without electricity.
Musk didn’t give a speech about this. He didn’t need to. He answered one question and the whole infrastructure myth collapsed.
“Where do you get the power plants from?”
Follow that thread far enough and you stop finding a technology problem.
You find a civilization that mastered thinking and forgot how to build.

summary:
Most current models that handle both image understanding and image generation rely on separate pretrained components: a vision encoder (a network like CLIP that turns images into feature vectors) for understanding, and a VAE — a compression network mapping images into a smaller latent representation — for generation.
The authors of this paper remove both and feed raw pixel patches directly into a single transformer trained end to end.
The results show that pretrained vision encoders are not necessary for multimodal modeling, and end-to-end pixel-space learning offers a scalable path toward stronger visual representations for both generation and perception.

In this paper, a 7B language model trained with reinforcement learning learns to orchestrate larger frontier models like GPT-5, Claude Sonnet 4, and Gemini 2.5 Pro.
It does so by writing natural-language subtasks, assigning each to one of the workers, and specifying which previous outputs that worker sees in context.
The resulting system outperforms every individual frontier model on benchmarks including GPQA Diamond, LiveCodeBench, and AIME25, while averaging about three model calls per question—fewer than the multi-agent pipelines and self-reflection loops it beats.
The work provides evidence that prompt engineering and pipeline design, currently done by hand in commercial AI products, can be learned end-to-end through reward signals alone.

clean_title: Impact of the prompt 'Let's think step by step' on LLM reasoning
summary:
This is the paper (obviously, from Google, again) that introduced, in 2022, before ChatGPT, the prompt "Let's think step by step" and showed it could pull multi-step reasoning out of a large language model without giving the model any worked examples first.
When a pretrained but not finetuned LLM is asked to solve a math word problem cold, it tends to output a wrong number directly; an earlier line of work fixed this by putting a handful of solved examples into the prompt that demonstrated the reasoning, a technique called chain-of-thought prompting.
Kojima and colleagues found that appending one fixed sentence — "Let's think step by step" — to any question, with no examples, moved accuracy on a math benchmark called MultiArith from 17.7% to 78.7% on a 175-billion-parameter model, with comparable jumps on grade-school math and on logic puzzles.
The same prompt works across arithmetic, symbolic, and other logical tasks, and the effect only appears once the model is large enough, which itself says something about what scale is doing.

clean_title: Scaling speech recognition training data to 680,000 hours
summary:
This paper documents what happens when speech recognition training data is scaled from the few thousand hours typical in academic work to 680,000 hours of audio scraped from the internet, paired with whatever transcripts happened to accompany it rather than carefully cleaned labels.
The resulting models, which became the OpenAI's Whisper system many people now use, work on audio they were never trained on with no finetuning on the target distribution, and the analyses explain why this matters in practice: models trained on a single clean dataset tend to absorb that dataset's idiosyncrasies, so they look superhuman on its test set while making roughly twice as many errors on other recordings.
The comparison against professional human transcribers on the same audio clearly illustrates the gap between in-distribution and out-of-distribution generalization, and it places a soft upper bound on how much further English transcription can improve along this path.
The experiments that vary dataset size and model size independently show where returns flatten, and where joint multilingual training stops hurting English performance and starts helping it, which is one of the more concrete pieces of evidence for positive transfer between languages at scale.

title: @burkov
clean_title: Memory module for language models that updates dynamically during conversation
summary:
The paper proposes a memory module that runs in parallel with a frozen language model rather than living inside its context window or in a separate retrieval database.
At each transformer layer where the module is inserted, it maintains a small matrix — eight by eight in their main setup — that gets updated as new tokens stream in, using a single gradient descent step on a small regression problem at each position: given a learned key vector, predict a learned value vector, and write back the prediction error into the matrix.
When the model generates, the current hidden state queries this matrix, and the readout is added as a small correction to the query and output vectors inside the model's attention computation.
The correction weights themselves are fixed after training, but because the matrix they read from changes continuously with the conversation, the same weights produce different behavior under different histories — which places the method in a different category than LoRA-style adapters, whose low-rank updates are static once training ends.
One experiment removes the source document from the prompt at test time, after the document has been streamed through the forward pass to update the per-layer matrices, and reports that multi-hop QA exact match rises from 0.08% to 6.48% — far below the score with the document still in the prompt, but well above chance, indicating the matrices carry enough signal to bias the frozen backbone's existing knowledge toward the right answers on a small fraction of questions.
Read with an AI tutor:
PDF:
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HIPiWmtXcAAiCgv.jpg

clean_title: Unifying framework for image generation methods in neural networks
summary:
There are two main families of methods for training neural networks to generate images. One steers random noise smoothly into a real-looking sample. The other learns to undo a process that gradually destroys data by adding noise.
They were developed separately, look different in the math, and come with different design choices — what noise schedule to use, whether to start from Gaussian noise specifically, when to make the generation process random versus deterministic.
This paper shows the two are really one construction with a choice attached: pick any path from noise to data you like, then decide separately whether to follow it smoothly or with random jitter.
The statistical behavior along the path is the same either way; only the individual sample trajectories differ.

There are two main families of methods for training neural networks to generate images. One method steers random noise smoothly into a real-looking sample, while the other learns to undo a process that gradually destroys data by adding noise. You can choose any path from noise to data and then decide whether to follow it smoothly or with random jitter. The statistical behavior along the path remains consistent, with only the individual sample trajectories differing.

clean_title: When can LLMs learn to reason with weak supervision?
summary:
A common story in recent AI work is that you can train an LLM to reason well even when the feedback during training is unreliable, a setting called "weak supervision."
In normal reinforcement learning for reasoning, a model attempts a problem and gets a reward signal telling it whether the answer was correct; weak supervision is when that signal is degraded in some way: only a handful of training problems are available, the correctness labels are mostly wrong, or there are no verified answers at all and the model has to fall back on judging its own outputs.
This Google, UCLA, and NYU paper looks at when training still works under those conditions and when it falls apart, and finds that the deciding factor is set before reinforcement learning even starts.
The authors track how quickly a model's training reward climbs to its ceiling, and show that models which reach the ceiling fast tend to memorize answers while models that climb slowly actually learn reasoning that transfers to new problems.

title: @burkov
clean_title: Detecting overfitting in neural networks during grokking using random matrix theory
summary:
Neural networks can overfit — they memorize the training data rather than learning a general rule, which makes them fail on new inputs. Everyone knows this, and the standard fix is to watch the gap between training accuracy and test accuracy during training.
This paper by @CalcCon and his collaborator focuses on a situation where that standard approach breaks down: you have a trained model's weights, no training history, no test set, and no idea whether the model learned something robust or something brittle.
The authors study a known phenomenon called grokking, where a model first memorizes, then much later suddenly generalizes — and they extend training even further to find a third phase where generalization collapses again while training accuracy stays perfect.
The two failure phases (before generalization, and after it collapses again) look identical from the outside but turn out to have a structural difference detectable directly in the weight matrices, without any data at all.
The detection method comes from random matrix theory: you shuffle each weight matrix element-by-element, build a covariance-type matrix from the shuffled weights, compute its eigenvalue spectrum, fit that spectrum to a known theoretical distribution, and look for eigenvalues that stick out well beyond where they should be.
In a well-trained model these don't appear; in an overfit one they do. The paper then applies this to two large open-weight models from OpenAI and finds the same signatures.
Learn from the paper with an AI tutor:
PDF:
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HIYXwYSWoAAQ03y.jpg
clean_summary:
Neural networks can overfit, memorizing training data instead of learning general rules, which leads to failure on new inputs. The standard fix is monitoring the gap between training and test accuracy, but this paper by @CalcCon and collaborators addresses a scenario where this approach fails: when only a trained model's weights are available, without training history or a test set.

The authors investigate grokking, a phenomenon where a model first memorizes and then later generalizes, extending their study to identify a third phase where generalization collapses again while training accuracy remains high. They reveal that the two failure phases appear identical externally but have a detectable structural difference in the weight matrices.

Using random matrix theory, the detection method involves shuffling weight matrix elements, constructing a covariance-type matrix, and analyzing its eigenvalue spectrum. In well-trained models, certain eigenvalues do not appear, while in overfit models, they do. The paper applies this method to two large open-weight models from OpenAI, confirming the presence of these signatures.

clean_title: Classifier-free guidance for text-to-image diffusion models
summary:
Generating an image from a sentence used to require a separate classifier trained on noisy images just to steer the output toward the prompt.
This paper from OpenAI shows you can drop that. The core idea is classifier-free guidance: during training the text caption is sometimes replaced with an empty one, so a single model learns to predict image noise both with and without text; at generation time you take the difference between the text-conditioned and unconditioned predictions and exaggerate it, which sharpens how closely the image follows the caption with no extra classifier.
The authors built a 3.5 billion parameter diffusion model around this, and human evaluators preferred its output to DALL-E (OpenAI's then-main system at twelve billion parameters) about 87% of the time for photorealism, even when DALL-E was allowed to generate many candidates and keep the best; they also finetuned the same model to fill erased image regions from a prompt, with matching shadows and reflections, making text-driven editing practical.
Classifier-free guidance went on to become standard and is still used in the systems leading the field in 2026 (FLUX.2, later Stable Diffusion, the models behind DALL-E 3 and Imagen).

📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HIgPkpVWgAAQJrG.png

clean_title: OpenHands: A software platform for AI agents to operate like developers
summary:
This ICLR 2025 paper documents OpenHands, a software platform that lets an AI agent operate a computer the way a developer does: writing and running code, issuing shell commands, and navigating web pages inside an isolated container.
The technical core is an event stream, which is simply a running log of every action the agent takes and every observation it gets back; the agent reads this history at each step and decides what to do next, so building a new agent reduces to writing one function that maps the current history to the next action.
Rather than giving the agent a fixed menu of tools, the design lets it express any action as ordinary Python or bash, which means new capabilities can be added as plain Python functions instead of being baked into the framework.
The authors also wire in fifteen existing evaluation benchmarks covering bug fixing, real GitHub issue resolution, web navigation, and tool use, and report how the same generalist agent does across all of them without per-task tuning.
The paper provides a concrete, implementation-level picture of how a code-executing agent is actually put together, including the parts usually left vague: how execution is sandboxed, how one agent hands a subtask to another, and how the team keeps agent behavior from silently regressing by recording and replaying model responses as deterministic tests.

title: @burkov
clean_title: Understanding the limitations of training policies on imagined experience in reinforcement learning
summary:
Modern reinforcement learning systems like Dreamer train policies entirely on imagined experience: a learned model predicts what the environment would do, a second learned model guesses what reward each imagined step would earn, and the policy improves from these fabricated trajectories without ever touching the real environment during the update.
When you train a policy on imagined experience, the policy ends up worse than if you'd trained it in the real world. The gap between "how good the policy looks in imagination" and "how good it actually is" comes from two separate mistakes: the dynamics model predicting the wrong next state, and the reward model predicting the wrong reward. Earlier theory mixed these together. This paper by @ylecun and colleagues pulls them apart, so you can see exactly how much of the damage comes from each one, and how much each can be controlled on its own.

clean_summary:
Modern reinforcement learning systems like Dreamer train policies entirely on imagined experience, where a learned model predicts environmental responses and another estimates rewards. However, training solely on imagined experience often results in worse policies compared to real-world training. The discrepancy arises from two separate errors: the dynamics model inaccurately predicting the next state and the reward model misestimating the reward. The paper by @ylecun and colleagues clarifies these issues by isolating the contributions of each error, allowing for better control over them.

title: @burkov
clean_title: VSI-Bench tests spatial reasoning in multimodal models
summary:
A model can describe a video of a room fluently, but does it actually hold a mental picture of where things are and how far apart they sit?
The authors of this CVPR 2025 Best Paper Candidate built VSI-Bench, a test of about 5,000 questions over roughly 290 real indoor videos, covering things like counting objects, judging which item is closest to another, estimating distances and room sizes, and recalling the order objects appeared.
They ran fifteen models through it and found that the best ones land well below people (about 79% for humans versus the mid-40s for the strongest model), but not at random either, so some spatial ability is present.
Asking the model to "think step by step," a prompting trick that usually helps with language and math, made spatial answers worse, not better, which points to spatial reasoning being a separate weakness rather than a reasoning-effort problem.
Furthermore, when the authors asked a model to sketch a rough grid map of object positions, it placed neighboring objects fairly well (around 64% correct) but degraded sharply for objects far apart, suggesting these models stitch together accurate local fragments without a single coherent map of the whole space; forcing the model to draw and then use such a map improved its distance answers.

PDF:
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HIkouxRXQAA17ch.jpg

title: @burkov
clean_title: Advancements in latent diffusion image generators with improved compression models
summary:
Latent diffusion image generators are built from two trained components: a compression model and a generator.
The compression model is trained on its own to take a picture, reduce it to a small set of numbers, and rebuild the original from those numbers as faithfully as possible; the generator then learns to produce pictures by producing those small numerical codes rather than raw pixels, and only its codes get expanded back into images, which is what keeps the computation manageable since a code can be hundreds of times smaller than the pixel grid.
The size of that code matters: the usual setup shrinks each image dimension by a factor of eight, but as target images get larger even that is not aggressive enough, and squeezing harder tends to destroy fine detail (text especially) while also leaving the code's statistics messy enough that the generator struggles to learn from them.
This May 2026 work from the Qwen team builds a family of compression models that shrink each dimension by sixteen or thirty-two times while keeping reconstruction sharp, combining three ideas.
The thirty-two-times model reaches text fidelity beating several sixteen-times competitors, and their sixteen-times model exceeds the standard eight-times baselines, which they report as the first result of its kind.

title: @burkov
clean_title: ModernBERT: An updated encoder model improving retrieval and classification
summary:
Most production systems that do retrieval or classification still run on BERT, a model released in 2018, even though the techniques used to build language models have changed substantially since then; the encoder family (models that read text and produce representations, rather than generating new text the way GPT-style models do) was largely left behind while attention went to large generative models.
The authors take the accumulated improvements from recent generative models—rotary positional embeddings (a way of encoding word order that extends cleanly to longer texts), gated activation functions, alternating local and global attention so most layers only look at nearby words while a few look at everything, and removal of padding tokens that waste computation—and apply them to encoder models, then train on 2 trillion tokens including code at a native context length of 8192 tokens (sixteen times BERT's 512-word limit).
The resulting models, ModernBERT-base and -large, do better than prior encoders across classification, single- and multi-vector retrieval, and code search, while processing long inputs roughly twice as fast as the next fastest competitor.
Since its December 2024 release, ModernBERT has become a widely adopted encoder backbone, with the approach extended into multilingual variants and broadly treated as the current default starting point for encoder-based retrieval and classification work.

title: @burkov
clean_title: GSM-Symbolic: A new approach to evaluating language model math skills
summary:
The standard way of measuring whether language models can do grade-school math may be misleading: GSM8K is a single fixed set of questions, so a high score could reflect memorization or contamination of the test data into training, and it gives no way to vary a question and see whether a model's competence holds up.
To get around this, the authors of this ICLR 2025 paper build GSM-Symbolic, where each original question becomes a template with named slots for people and numbers plus rules that keep the answer valid, so they can generate many versions of the same underlying problem and look at performance as a spread of scores rather than a single number.
Running this across more than twenty open and closed models, they find that scores swing noticeably just from changing names or values even though the reasoning needed stays identical, that the original GSM8K score usually sits at the high end of this spread (which fits the contamination worry), and that accuracy falls and becomes more erratic as more clauses are added to a problem.
Their sharpest result comes from GSM-NoOp, where they insert a sentence that sounds relevant but changes nothing about the math; models routinely fold that sentence into a calculation anyway, with drops as large as 65 percent, and giving them worked examples of the same question does not fix it, which points toward pattern matching rather than genuine step-by-step reasoning.

PDF:
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HIknuZOWwAA-YpB.png

summary:
Most systems that let an AI agent split a hard problem into pieces and hand those pieces to fresh copies of itself treat that splitting as scaffolding bolted onto a model that was never trained to do it, so the model is left guessing about when delegating helps, how to phrase a subtask, and how to combine what comes back.
This 2026 paper from Amazon and CMU trains a single language model to make those decisions itself: the same model runs at every node of a tree of delegated subtasks, and learning happens through reinforcement learning.
The central design choice is a local reward—each node is scored on whether its own assigned task succeeded plus a bonus for how often its delegated children succeeded, which lets the model learn decomposition even before it can solve the full task.
An agent trained with an 8K-token context window solves crafting tasks that exceed that window (95% versus 24% for a non-recursive baseline), a 30B model approaches the long-document performance of larger frontier systems, and the recursion the model learns is adaptive, going deeper on harder problems and staying shallow when one round of splitting suffices.

clean_title: Adaptive language models with separate fast prompt updates and slow weight changes
summary:
When a language model is finetuned for a task like math or coding through reinforcement learning, every lesson it learns has to be written into the same set of weights that holds everything else the model knows, which means improving at the new task also pushes the model away from its original behavior, narrows the range of outputs it will produce, and weakens its ability to learn the next task it encounters.
This paper proposes adapting the model along two separate channels that change at different speeds. The first is the model weights, the billions of numbers fixed during training, which move slowly through reinforcement learning.
The second is the prompt: the block of instruction text placed in front of the model's actual question, separate from the weights and made only of words, which can therefore be swapped for a better version immediately and at almost no cost compared to retraining.
The authors improve both at once in alternating rounds, rather than tuning the prompt only after training finishes, so the prompt absorbs fast, task-specific corrections while the weights stay closer to where they started.
Across code, math, and fact-verification tasks they show this reaches the same accuracy as reinforcement learning alone with up to three times fewer training examples, settles at a higher final accuracy, keeps the trained model measurably closer to the base model, and leaves the model still able to learn a second, different task afterward, whereas a model trained with reinforcement learning alone sometimes drops to near-zero accuracy when asked to learn something new.

PDF:
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HIqQXeeXwAANwnO.jpg

clean_title: OP-MIX: a unified method for data mixing throughout a model's lifecycle
summary:
Training a language model normally happens in separate stages—first pretraining on a broad corpus, then later adding new data for specialized skills—and each stage has historically used its own method for deciding how much of each data source to include in the training mix.
Those methods are expensive: the common trick is to train many small stand-in models on different data recipes and extrapolate, which becomes combinatorially costly as the number of data sources grows, and most of these methods also assume the set of data sources is fixed, so they break down once new datasets arrive after pretraining is finished.
This 2026 paper from CMU and Microsoft argues that choosing a data mix is really one recurring decision throughout a model's whole life, and it introduces a single method, OP-MIX, that handles it everywhere.
The core trick uses a low-rank adapter—a small set of extra weights trained on top of a frozen base model, far cheaper than training the full model—to stand in for what full training on a given data source would produce; the authors then mathematically blend (interpolate) these adapters to simulate many different data mixes using only forward passes, with no extra training runs and no separate stand-in models.
They show this one method reaches or beats specialized baselines across pretraining, mid-training, and instruction tuning while spending a fraction of the compute, including matching a more elaborate continual-learning technique with 95% less compute, and they back the empirical results with a clean error analysis bounding how far the method's chosen mix can fall from optimal.

title: @burkov
clean_title: On-Policy Distillation of Language Models: Learning from Self-Generated Mistakes
summary:
An absolute must read.
LLMs cost a lot to run, so a common move is to train a small model to imitate a big one — feeding the small "student" the same inputs and having it match, word by word, the probabilities the large "teacher" assigns to each possible next word, a procedure called knowledge distillation.
That matching is done on a fixed collection of example sentences, but a model writing text builds each sentence out of its own earlier words, so once the student makes an early choice that none of the training examples contained, it ends up in situations it was never shown, and small mistakes feed into later ones until the text degrades.
In this ICLR 2024 paper from Google, Mila, and UoT, the authors instead have the student write sentences itself and use those sentences to choose the situations it gets tested on: at each point in a student-written sentence they take the words so far, ask the teacher what the distribution over the next word should be there, and push the student toward the teacher's answer — so the teacher supplies every target while the student's own writing decides where those targets get applied, which is exactly the off-track spots its writing tends to wander into.
Tested on summarization, English-to-German translation, and grade-school math problems where the model writes out its reasoning before answering, this self-generated-data approach beats standard distillation recipes across a range of student sizes, and it slots into reinforcement-learning fine-tuning cleanly because both only need samples drawn from the student rather than gradients passed back through the sampling step.
Read with an AI tutor and quizzes for better retention:
PDF:
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HItQlpKWcAMsERU.jpg
clean_summary:
Large language models are expensive to run, so a common approach is to train smaller models to imitate larger ones through knowledge distillation. Traditional distillation uses fixed example sentences, but this can lead to errors accumulating when the student generates text out of its training distribution.

A new approach from an ICLR 2024 paper by Google, Mila, and UoT has the student write sentences itself and uses those sentences to determine the test situations. At each step in a student-generated sentence, the teacher provides the next-word distribution based on the current context, guiding the student toward accurate predictions. This method, tested on tasks like summarization, translation, and math reasoning, outperforms standard distillation across various model sizes. It also integrates smoothly with reinforcement learning fine-tuning because it only requires samples from the student, not gradients through the sampling process.

title: @burkov
clean_title: The Hundred-Page Language Models Book by Andriy Burkov
summary:
The Hundred-Page Language Models Book is a strong book. It's the third in Andriy Burkov's series of AI textbooks, following The Hundred-Page Machine Learning Book and Machine Learning Engineering, both of which became #1 bestsellers. It currently sits at about 4.49 out of 5 on Goodreads, and reception from practitioners has been broadly positive.
What it actually is
It's a concise (~150 pages despite the "hundred-page" branding) progressive walk from machine learning fundamentals to modern LLMs. The structure is deliberately bottom-up: it covers machine learning basics, language modeling basics, recurrent neural networks, the Transformer, and large language models across six chapters. The pedagogical bet is that revisiting older approaches like count-based methods and RNNs first builds intuition so the Transformer feels like a natural progression rather than an intimidating leap. It also touches practical concerns like hallucinations and model evaluation, with full code available through the book's wiki, and all code examples run on Google Colab.
The case for it
The author's reputation rests on a specific skill: compression without dumbing down. One endorser captured the recurring praise — that Burkov has a talent for shrinking large AI concepts into bite-sized "now I get it" moments. A reader review echoed the practitioner consensus: it blends theory, math, and practical PyTorch code clearly, and tackles real topics like finetuning and model evaluation without getting bogged down, with the balance between theory and practice being about right. The hands-on, code-from-scratch approach (you build and train three architectures of language models, including coding a Transformer in PyTorch) is what differentiates it from purely conceptual treatments. The endorsement list is heavyweight: a foreword by Tomáš Mikolov (word2vec author) and back-cover text by Vint Cerf.
Who it's good for
It's an excellent fit if you're a software engineer or data scientist with Python experience who wants to genuinely understand how language models work under the hood — not just call an API — and you value a tight, buildable mental model you can read in a week. It's a weaker fit if you're a true beginner wanting gentle hand-holding, or an experienced ML practitioner wanting cutting-edge depth on training and serving production LLMs. For the former, a longer introductory text serves better; for the latter, this is a fast refresher rather than new ground.

Training loss falls smoothly while a model learns, which makes it tempting to treat it as a full report on what is happening inside the network, but two runs that reach the same loss can have very different internal organization, and loss alone hides this.

They then back the empirical claims with a small modular-arithmetic model where the relevant features are known by construction, so the spectral shifts can be tied directly to which task-relevant features the network has actually picked up.
The practical payoff is a cheap early signal for choosing batch size and judging architectural tweaks without running every configuration to completion.

clean_title: Evaluating language models as judges: challenges and failure modes
summary:
Word-overlap metrics like BLEU and ROUGE fail on open-ended text, where two good answers can share little vocabulary and qualities like helpfulness or safety don't reduce to matching word sequences, so researchers now use language models themselves as graders — but the practice has spread across evaluation, alignment data generation, retrieval ranking, and reasoning-step scoring without a shared vocabulary.
The authors organize the field along three axes: what gets judged (helpfulness, safety, faithfulness, relevance, logical correctness, overall quality), how judging is set up (finetuning on preference labels versus inference-time tricks like swapping candidate order to cancel position bias, embedding rubrics, or running judges as a debating panel), and how to benchmark the judges themselves.
They also document recurring failure modes — judges preferring longer or more authoritative-sounding answers, favoring outputs from their own model family, and being steerable through prompt injection — which is the part most directly useful for anyone currently relying on a model-graded leaderboard.

summary:
Specialized time series models are good at picking up seasonal patterns and trends from raw numbers but have no way to react to events described in news or reports, while large language models can read that text and reason about it but are weak at the actual numerical extrapolation.
Most attempts to combine the two either glue a language model onto numerical data through heavy retraining or use one giant prompt that asks a single model to do everything at once, and the authors from Google and Penn State argue this is the wrong decomposition.
Their contribution is Nexus, a system that splits forecasting into separate cooperating agents (each agent is just a language model given a specific role and prompt): one cleans the messy mix of numbers and text into a structured timeline, one produces a broad long-range outlook, one walks step by step through near-term changes, and a final agent merges these into a single forecast, with an added loop that tests the system's past errors on held-out historical splits and writes down correction rules only if they actually improve accuracy.
Tested on stock prices and Zillow housing data drawn entirely from after the models' knowledge cutoff (so the models could not have memorized the answers), this arrangement matches or beats both a strong dedicated time series model and a single-prompt language model baseline, and it produces written explanations of why each forecast moves the way it does, which the authors check using one model family to judge the other.

title: @burkov
clean_title: LLMs as components of AI agent systems: scaffolding, mechanisms, and scaling
summary:
LLMs have moved from producing standalone code to powering AI agents — systems that plan over many steps, call external tools, keep track of changing state, and recover from their own errors during long-running tasks.
Inside these systems, code has become the working material for almost everything: agents write small programs to reason through math, to drive a browser, to query a database, to test their own outputs, and to share intermediate work with other agents through files in a repository.
Existing surveys still treat code mainly as the final answer that a model produces. The authors of this paper argue this misses the broader role code now plays inside agent systems.
They use the term "agent harness" for the scaffolding around a model (planning, memory, tool calls, and execution-based verification loops) that turns one-shot generation into something that can run for hours on a real task, and they organize their map of this scaffolding into three connected layers: the interface, covering how code lets an agent reason, act, and represent its environment; the mechanisms, covering how planning, memory, tool use, and feedback-driven repair keep long executions on track; and the scaling layer, covering how several agents share repositories, tests, and execution traces to coordinate.
Each layer is tied to concrete systems such as Claude Code and Codex, and to application areas including software engineering, GUI and OS automation, embodied robots, scientific discovery, and personalization.

Large language models have shifted from generating standalone code to powering complex AI agents that plan over multiple steps, call external tools, track changing states, and recover from errors during long tasks.

Within these systems, code serves as the core material for reasoning, acting, and environment representation. The 'agent harness' refers to the scaffolding around a model—such as planning, memory, tool use, and verification loops—that enables continuous operation over hours. This scaffolding is organized into three layers: the interface, which connects code to reasoning and action; the mechanisms, which include planning, feedback, and tool integration to maintain long-term execution; and the scaling layer, where multiple agents share repositories, tests, and traces for coordination.

These layers relate to systems like Claude Code and Codex and apply across domains like software engineering, automation, robotics, scientific discovery, and personalization. Recognizing code's broader role inside agent systems highlights its importance beyond just final outputs, emphasizing its function in enabling sustained, adaptable AI behavior.

title: @burkov
clean_title: Recursive reasoning models with stochastic updates for improved problem-solving
summary:
Most reasoning systems built on LLMs scale by generating longer chains of intermediate text, one token at a time. A different family of methods, called recursive reasoning models, keeps a small internal state vector and repeatedly updates it using the same neural network weights, so the depth of reasoning comes from the number of update iterations rather than the length of generated output.
Recent examples like HRM and TRM do well on hard puzzles such as Sudoku-Extreme and ARC-AGI, but for a given input they always perform the exact same sequence of updates and converge to a single answer, which is a poor fit for problems with many valid solutions, or where the first refinement path leads to a dead end.
The authors of this paper modify the update rule so that at each iteration a small Gaussian perturbation, whose mean and variance the model learns to predict from the current state, is added to the hidden state, turning the deterministic recursion into a distribution over possible reasoning trajectories.
On Sudoku, running 20 short stochastic trajectories in parallel matches or beats one very long deterministic trajectory at comparable compute, giving a "width" axis along which inference can be scaled in addition to depth, and the same architecture run with no input behaves as a generative model that produces valid 9×9 Sudoku boards from a blank grid 99% of the time, ahead of diffusion baselines that use roughly five times as many parameters and a thousand denoising steps.

Recent examples like HRM and TRM perform well on challenging puzzles such as Sudoku-Extreme and ARC-AGI, but they always follow the same sequence of updates for a given input, which limits their ability to handle problems with many valid solutions or where early refinements lead to dead ends. This approach enables more flexible and scalable reasoning, with potential applications in problem-solving and generative modeling.

title: @burkov
clean_title: PTRM improves accuracy of small recursive models on reasoning puzzles
summary:
Small recursive models like TRM solve hard reasoning puzzles using only about 7 million parameters by repeatedly refining a hidden internal state and the predicted answer — a different style of computation than the token-by-token generation used by large language models.
But this refinement is deterministic, so when the model settles on a wrong answer there is no mechanism to escape it, while LLMs can be sampled many times and combined through voting.
The authors visualize what TRM does across its refinement steps and find that many failures correspond to trajectories trapped in regions of the hidden state space that decode to incorrect answers, when a small change in path would have led to the right solution.
They also notice that TRM already contains a "Q head" — a small auxiliary output trained alongside the main network to estimate whether the current answer is correct, originally used only at training time to halt computation on already-solved examples — and that this head separates correct from incorrect trajectories reliably enough to serve as a verifier at inference time.
Their method, PTRM, adds Gaussian noise (random numbers drawn from a bell curve centered at zero) to the hidden state at each refinement step, runs K such perturbed copies in parallel, and picks the answer with the highest Q score.
Without any retraining or task-specific modifications, this raises accuracy on Sudoku-Extreme from 87.4% to 98.75% and on a set of pencil puzzles from 62.6% to 91.2%, outperforming an ensemble of seven frontier LLMs at less than one ten-thousandth of the cost.

title: @burkov
clean_title: Backlash against AI among LinkedIn white-collar workers
summary:
A huge backlash against AI among the white collars on LinkedIn.
I have a newsletter there that has been covering all things AI for more than 7 years. The content is purely educational, no rumors or mergers/acquisitions.
The first several years since creation was an explosive growth. Two years ago, the newsletter reached 850,000 subscribers and every month several thousand more subscribed.
Each issue got nearly 500 likes and other reactions.
Since about a year things started to change. The likes fell first to 250, then to 100, and now are around 75 per issue.
But what the most alarming is that people started to unsubscribe. Today, the number if subscribers fell below 850k for the first time since 2024.
My conclusion is that white collar workers aka knowledge workers used to see AI knowledge as a competitive advantage and wanted to absorb as much knowledge as possible. Not anymore.
The posts on LinkedIn that get the most support are those where AI is shown to be dumb, products built with it useless and buggy, and people using it incompetent.
If I had to choose one person to blame for this change of heart, is Amodei. No one spoke about his AI to replace all white collar professionals as this dumb and irresponsible individual with a big mouth and no filter.
clean_summary:
A long-standing AI newsletter on LinkedIn, which grew rapidly over the years, is now experiencing a decline in engagement and subscribers. Likes per issue have dropped from nearly 500 to around 75, and unsubscribe rates have increased, with subscriber numbers falling below 850,000 for the first time since 2024.

The shift suggests that knowledge workers no longer see AI as a competitive advantage. Instead, the most supported posts highlight AI's failures, such as buggy products and incompetent usage. The change is attributed to concerns raised by Amodei, who is criticized for promoting an irresponsible view of AI replacing white-collar professionals.

title: @burkov
clean_title: Classical planning in deep latent space with learned symbolic representations
summary:
Classical AI planners can find optimal solutions to combinatorial problems like sliding-tile puzzles in milliseconds, but only if a human first writes the problem out in a symbolic language such as PDDL that names every proposition and every action together with its preconditions and effects.
This requirement has kept symbolic planning largely separate from raw sensor data such as photographs, where there are no pre-existing symbols, only pixels. The authors of this paper build a system called Latplan that learns the symbolic representation on its own from nothing more than unlabeled pairs of before-and-after images of the environment, then hands the learned model to an off-the-shelf planner like Fast Downward.
The core construction is a discrete autoencoder — a neural network that compresses an input into a smaller representation and reconstructs it, where the compressed representation is forced to be a vector of 0/1 bits rather than real numbers — that maps each image to a binary state vector whose individual bits act as propositions, paired with a second network that learns action effects in a form matching STRIPS rules, meaning each action sets a fixed set of bits to true and another fixed set to false regardless of the rest of the state, so the result can be exported directly as PDDL.
Read with an AI tutor and quizzes for better retention:

clean_summary:
Classical AI planners can quickly find optimal solutions to combinatorial problems like sliding-tile puzzles, but they require a human to first encode the problem symbolically, which limits their application to raw sensor data like images. This work introduces Latplan, a system that learns symbolic representations directly from unlabeled pairs of before-and-after environment images, enabling the use of standard planners without manual encoding.

Latplan uses a discrete autoencoder—a neural network that compresses images into binary state vectors, where each bit acts as a proposition. A second network learns action effects in a form matching STRIPS rules, where actions set specific bits to true or false, allowing the learned model to be exported as PDDL. This approach bridges raw sensory data and symbolic planning, making classical planning applicable to unstructured inputs.

title: @burkov
clean_title: Residual connections as diffusion models enable block-wise training of deep neural networks
summary:
Training a deep neural network with standard backpropagation requires keeping every layer's intermediate activations in memory until the backward pass uses them, so memory grows with depth and limits how large models can be made.
Previous attempts to split a network into pieces that train independently have been ad-hoc, performed noticeably worse than ordinary training, or only worked on classification tasks.
The authors of this ICLR 2026 paper notice that a residual connection (where a layer adds its output to its input instead of replacing it) is mathematically identical to one step of a diffusion model — a generative model trained by adding noise to data and learning to remove that noise step by step.
Since each noise level in a diffusion model can be trained on its own without depending on the others, the authors use this correspondence to partition a transformer into blocks, assign each block a range of noise levels, and train every block on its own denoising objective with no gradient flow between blocks.
Memory during training shrinks by a factor equal to the number of blocks, since only one block holds gradients at a time, and the same recipe works across vision transformers, image diffusion models, autoregressive language models, masked diffusion, and recurrent-depth models, matching ordinary end-to-end training in most cases and exceeding it in some.
Read with an AI tutor and quizzes for better retention:
PDF:
clean_summary: Training deep neural networks with standard backpropagation requires storing all intermediate activations, which causes memory growth with depth and limits model size. Previous methods to train networks in pieces often performed worse or only worked on specific tasks. This work observes that residual connections in transformers are mathematically equivalent to one step of a diffusion model, a generative process that learns to denoise data at different noise levels. By exploiting this analogy, the authors partition a transformer into blocks, assign each block a range of noise levels, and train each block independently on a denoising objective without gradient flow between blocks. This approach reduces memory during training proportionally to the number of blocks and works across various model types, matching or exceeding the performance of end-to-end training in most cases.

clean_title: Superposition explains the power-law loss scaling in large language models
summary:
LLMs reliably score lower loss, and the loss drops as a smooth power of model size, but nobody had pinned down what physical thing inside the network produces that particular curve.
This MIT paper proposes an answer rooted in superposition, the trick by which a network packs more distinct features into its hidden space than it has dimensions, by letting feature directions overlap a little rather than sit perfectly perpendicular.
Read with an AI tutor:
PDF:
clean_summary:
Large language models (LLMs) reliably achieve lower loss as they grow in size, following a smooth power-law curve. However, the underlying physical mechanism inside the network that produces this specific pattern was not previously understood.

This MIT paper suggests that superposition, the technique by which a network encodes more features than its dimensions by allowing feature directions to overlap slightly, accounts for this phenomenon. Instead of features being perfectly orthogonal, they overlap a little, enabling the network to pack more information into its hidden space while maintaining robustness.

The work connects the loss scaling behavior to the concept of superposition, providing a physical explanation for the observed power-law reduction in loss as models grow larger.

clean_title: Google's Gemini model adapts into a unified embedding system for multimodal data
summary:
Most systems that handle different kinds of data—text, images, video, audio—do so by training a separate encoder for each type and then forcing their outputs into a shared space, which works for matching an image to a caption but loses the connections that arise when those types appear together, as in a video with narration or a document mixing charts and prose.
This recent work from Google takes a model already trained to understand all these types at once (Gemini) and adapts it into an embedding model, meaning one that turns any input into a single fixed-length vector of numbers whose geometric closeness reflects semantic similarity, so that related items end up near each other regardless of which modality they came from.
The authors do this through contrastive training, where the model is shown matched pairs and learns to pull them close while pushing unrelated items apart, run in stages across many tasks and modalities, and they report that the single resulting model matches or beats specialized systems on text retrieval, image-text matching, video search, code search, and audio retrieval.
Two specifics stand out: feeding raw audio directly into the model retrieves text better than first transcribing the audio into words and embedding that; and the model holds up across narrow fields it was not specifically trained on, from microscopy images to paintings to recipes, where competing models swing between strong and weak depending on the domain.
Read with an AI tutor:
PDF:
clean_summary:
Most systems that handle different types of data—such as text, images, video, and audio—train separate encoders for each modality and then map their outputs into a shared space. This approach works for matching images to captions but loses the connections when multiple types appear together, like in videos with narration or documents with charts and prose.

Recent work from Google transforms the Gemini model, which is trained to understand all these modalities simultaneously, into an embedding model. This model converts any input into a fixed-length vector, where the proximity of vectors reflects their semantic similarity across modalities. It uses contrastive training with matched pairs to learn to bring related items closer and push unrelated ones apart, across many tasks and modalities.

The results show that this single model can match or outperform specialized systems on tasks like text retrieval, image-text matching, video search, code search, and audio retrieval. Notably, feeding raw audio directly into the model yields better text retrieval than transcribing audio first. The model also performs well in domains it wasn't specifically trained on, such as microscopy images, paintings, and recipes, where other models' performance varies significantly. This work demonstrates a versatile, unified approach to multimodal understanding that can handle diverse data types efficiently.

title: @burkov
clean_title: Self-prediction of internal representations reduces data needs in hierarchical models
summary:
LLMs and image generators need much more training data than a human child does to reach comparable competence, and one explanation is that predicting raw tokens—the next word, a masked pixel—wastes effort on surface details rather than the abstract structure underneath.
Some recent methods instead train a network to predict its own internal representations of the data, but there has been little theory saying how much this helps or why.
The authors of this paper study this using a synthetic language model called the Random Hierarchy Model, where data is built by a tree of hidden symbols of depth L: visible tokens at the bottom, increasingly abstract latent symbols above, with fixed random rules connecting each level to the next.
Within this setting they can count exactly how many training examples a method needs to recover the hidden tree. Standard supervised learning and token-level prediction need a number of samples that grows exponentially with the depth L, because the statistical signal connecting a token to distant parts of the tree gets averaged away across many levels.
The authors prove that predicting one's own latents instead needs a number of samples that does not grow with depth at all (roughly m³, where m is the number of rules per symbol), because once a level has been decoded the next level becomes just as easy to learn as the first—every level reduces to the same local problem.
clean_summary:
LLMs and image generators require much more training data than humans to achieve similar competence. One reason is that predicting raw tokens focuses on surface details rather than the underlying abstract structure. Recent methods train networks to predict their own internal representations, but there has been little theory explaining how much this helps.

Using a synthetic language model called the Random Hierarchy Model, where data is generated by a tree of hidden symbols with fixed random rules, the authors analyze how many training examples are needed for different methods to recover the hidden structure. They find that standard supervised learning and token-level prediction require exponentially more samples as the depth of the hierarchy increases, because the signal gets diluted across levels. In contrast, predicting one's own latents needs a number of samples that does not grow with depth, roughly proportional to the cube of the number of rules per symbol, because once a level is decoded, the next level becomes just as easy to learn as the first, reducing the problem to a local one.

clean_title: Using per-user adapters to personalize shared language models
summary:
Most work on parameter-efficient finetuning treats it as a way to save money: instead of retraining all of a large model's weights, you train a small set of extra weights (an "adapter," with LoRA being the common method) and leave the original model frozen.
The authors of this paper explore whether such an adapter could be the place where a model stores who one particular user is over time, while millions of users share one underlying model the way billions of people share almost the same genome and differ in a tiny fraction of it.
The authors organize the argument around three connected questions and back each with experiments: whether a stronger shared model makes small adapters more useful; how small an adapter can get before it stops learning reliably; and what becomes possible with many adapters at once (they measure how much an adapter can hold as memory, use per-user adapters to make crowd simulations behave like distinct people rather than one model wearing costumes, and show that voting across 198 differently-trained adapters lifts math accuracy from about 36% to 49%).

clean_title: Measuring Effective Feedback Compute to Improve System Success
summary:
When people build systems where a language model works through a problem by repeatedly calling tools, checking its own work, and revising, the natural way to measure effort is to count tokens used, tool calls made, or money spent.
But two runs with the same token count can differ significantly in whether anything useful actually happened: one might gather solid evidence and remember it, while the other spins in circles repeating the same failed attempt.
The authors of this paper propose measuring the Effective Feedback Compute—a number that gives credit to a piece of feedback only when it tells the system something new, comes from a reliable source like a passing test, is relevant to what the system is currently trying to do, and actually gets retained and used in later steps.
They also divide this number by a measure of how much feedback a given task demands in the first place, since an easy task and a hard one need different amounts.
Across made-up tasks where they can see the hidden answer, coding tasks checked by real tests, and traces from existing benchmarks, this measure tracks how often systems fail far better than counting raw spending does, and they show with carefully matched experiments that holding the budget fixed while improving feedback quality raises success from 27 to 90 percent, which rules out the explanation that more feedback just means more spending.

When building systems where a language model solves problems by repeatedly calling tools, checking its work, and revising, effort is often measured by tokens used, tool calls, or money spent. However, two runs with the same token count can differ greatly in usefulness: one might gather and remember solid evidence, while the other repeats failures.

The paper proposes the Effective Feedback Compute, a metric that credits feedback only when it provides new, reliable, relevant, and retained information that aids later steps. This measure is then normalized by the feedback demand of the task, recognizing that easier and harder tasks require different amounts of feedback.

Experiments on synthetic tasks, coding challenges with real tests, and benchmark traces show that this feedback quality measure better predicts failure rates than raw spending. Fixing the budget and improving feedback quality raises success rates from 27% to 90%, demonstrating that better feedback, not just more spending, drives system improvement.

title: @burkov
clean_title: Vector Policy Optimization for Diverse Trade-offs in Language Model Training
summary:
Most RL for language models pushes a model toward the single answer that scores highest on some reward, and a known side effect is that the model's outputs become nearly identical to each other after training; this matters because language models are now often run inside a search loop, where the system generates many candidate answers to the same problem and a cheap checker (running a program's test cases, verifying a final numeric result) keeps the best one.
This works because for hard problems a single attempt often fails, but sampling many attempts and checking each one reliably finds a correct attempt, and checking is far cheaper than generating, so the expensive generation step can be run many times in parallel.
Such a loop only helps if the candidates actually differ from each other, which is the problem the side effect above creates: you pay to generate many answers but get the variety of roughly one.
The authors of this paper notice that rewards in real tasks are usually made of several separate parts rather than one number (for code, whether each individual test case passes; for multi-step question answering, whether each step is correct), and they use this structure: during training they repeatedly draw a random set of weights that combine those parts into a single score in different ways, ask the model to produce several answers in one pass, and reward the model based on how well its best answer does under each random weighting, which pressures the different answers to specialize toward different trade-offs instead of collapsing together.
Their method, Vector Policy Optimization, swaps directly into a standard training algorithm (GRPO) by changing only how the reward is computed, and across four tasks plus a coding benchmark it matches or beats the usual approach once you let the search loop draw more candidates, even solving hard programming problems that the standard model couldn't solve.
clean_summary: Most reinforcement learning for language models encourages the model to produce a single answer that scores highest on some reward, which often leads to outputs becoming nearly identical after training. This is problematic because in search loops, generating many diverse candidate answers is crucial for finding correct solutions efficiently, especially when checking is cheaper than generation. The paper observes that real task rewards are usually composed of multiple parts, such as passing individual test cases or verifying each step in multi-step questions. It proposes a method called Vector Policy Optimization, which during training randomly weights these parts to create different composite scores, encouraging the model to produce answers that specialize toward different trade-offs rather than collapsing into one. This approach, integrated into standard training algorithms by changing only the reward calculation, matches or surpasses traditional methods across several tasks and even solves difficult programming problems that previous models could not.

clean_title: The Hundred-Page Machine Learning Book by Andriy Burkov
summary:
The Hundred-Page Machine Learning Book by Andriy Burkov is widely regarded as a good book.
Ruthless signal-to-noise ratio. Burkov made a deliberate editorial choice to include only what matters and cut everything else. There's no padding, no filler anecdotes, no 30-page warm-ups before the real content. Every paragraph is doing work. This respects your time in a way most textbooks don't, and it means you can actually finish it—unlike the 800-page tomes that sit half-read on shelves.
It gives you the map before the territory. The book's real value is structural: it shows how the pieces of ML fit together as a coherent whole. You come away understanding where SVMs sit relative to logistic regression, how regularization connects to the bias-variance tradeoff, why gradient descent underlies so much of the field. That scaffolding is exactly what's hard to build when you learn topics piecemeal from scattered tutorials, and it's what makes everything you learn afterward stick better.
The math is present but proportionate. Burkov includes the linear algebra, probability, and calculus you actually need to understand the algorithms—derivations of gradient descent, the intuition behind kernels, the probabilistic reasoning under Naive Bayes—without drowning you in proofs. It's enough to make the methods feel principled rather than magical, but not so much that the math becomes the obstacle.
Practitioner-grade priorities. The book spends real estate on things working ML people care about: feature engineering, handling imbalanced data, hyperparameter tuning, regularization, model evaluation and metrics, the difference between what works in a paper and what works in production. This is hard-won practical judgment, not just textbook theory, and it's the part that's genuinely useful when you sit down to build something.
Writing quality and credibility. title: @burkov
clean_title: Trajectory-Refined Distillation for Correcting Prefix Failures in Language Models
summary:
Assume you are training a small language model by having a larger "teacher" model correct it token by token along the small model's own attempts at solving a problem. A specific thing goes wrong that the authors of this 2026 paper from McGill, Mila and UT Austin name prefix failure: once the student starts down a wrong reasoning path, the teacher faces an awkward choice at every following word, either continuing the doomed path the student committed to or abruptly pivoting back toward the correct answer, and this split makes the correction signal weak and scattered rather than useful.
The authors show that the standard fixes people use (reweighting or capping individual token corrections) cannot repair this because they operate on the wrong scale: the failed reasoning prefix stays in place no matter how you adjust the per-token corrections, so the teacher just keeps pointing at the same "wait, this is wrong" word over and over on top of an already-broken context.
Their proposed method, Trajectory-Refined Distillation, changes what the student learns from: instead of correcting the student's flawed attempt in place, the teacher first rewrites the whole attempt into a cleaner version that fixes the errors while staying close to how the student tends to reason, and the student then learns from that rewritten version, which also exposes it to shorter and alternative valid solutions even on problems it already solves.
clean_summary:
Training small language models with a larger teacher model can face a problem called prefix failure, where once the student starts down a wrong reasoning path, the teacher struggles to provide effective correction signals. Standard fixes like reweighting or capping token corrections fail because they operate on the wrong scale, leaving the failed prefix unchanged and causing the teacher to repeatedly point at the same incorrect word.

The proposed method, Trajectory-Refined Distillation, addresses this by having the teacher rewrite the entire attempt into a cleaner version that corrects errors while maintaining the student's reasoning style. The student then learns from this rewritten version, which exposes it to shorter and alternative solutions, improving its ability to recover from mistakes and generate better reasoning paths.

title: @burkov
clean_title: Transformers struggle with state tracking due to unidirectional information flow
summary:
Transformers keep their entire input history available and can look back into it for any fact, which suits retrieval but doesn't work well with a task the authors call state tracking.
Imagine a model playing a guessing game: after each guess it says "higher" or "lower," so it must carry along the range the hidden number could still be in and narrow that range with every guess.
That range is a running summary the model has to keep and revise as the conversation goes; each guess moves it one step forward; and each narrowed range is computed from the previous range plus the latest guess, so the values form a chain, every one depending on the last.
In this recent arXiv paper from Google, the authors show transformers handle this badly: a model gives contradictory hints in this game or could flips between the two meanings of "bank" mid-conversation.
The reason is in how the information flows in a transformer. As a transformer reads input, it holds a separate vector of numbers for every word at every layer of the network, and information only ever flows upward through the layers, never back down—so once the model computes the current range and parks it at some layer, the next range, which depends on that one, can only land at the same layer or deeper, never shallower.
Each step pushes the running summary one level up the stack, and since the stack has a fixed number of layers, a long enough conversation runs it off the top with nowhere left to put the next update.
The author argue that a proper state tracking needs recurrence—feeding a deep representation back down to a shallow one, as older recurrent networks did—and explain why this implicit recurrence beats making a model "think out loud" in extra tokens for routine bookkeeping.
clean_summary: Transformers keep their entire input history available and can look back into it for facts, which suits retrieval tasks but not state tracking. In a recent arXiv paper from Google, it is shown that transformers handle this poorly because their information flows only upward through layers, preventing the model from revisiting and revising earlier representations. This causes contradictions in tasks like a guessing game where the model must maintain and update a running range, as the fixed number of layers limits how much the model can revise its internal state over long conversations. The authors argue that effective state tracking requires recurrence—feeding deep representations back down to earlier layers—something that implicit recurrence in recurrent networks accomplishes better than just making the model 'think out loud' with extra tokens.

title: @burkov
summary:
It's well known that Russian is a very difficult language to learn because of too many rules and even more exceptions from these rules, but even within this obvious difficulty, there's one thing that makes even me, a native speaker, crazy when I think about it.
In many languages, possessive pronouns change depending on the gender of the possessed object. For example, in French, you say "ta" (your) when the next word is feminine like "ta maison" (your house) or "ton" when the next word is masculine like "ton bateau" (your boat). Then, for "my" you would use, based on the same principle, "ma/mon" for feminine/masculine nouns and for "his/hers/its" you would use "sa/son".
In Russian, for "your" and "my," you would use "твоя" (your) or "моя" (my) for "рука" (hand) because "рука" is feminine, and you would use "мой" and "твой" for "дом" (house) because "дом" is masculine, BUT you would use "его" (his) for nouns of any gender when the possessor is male, and you would use "её" (her) for nouns of any gender because the possessor is female.
So, as a foreign language learner, you must not only remember by heart the gender of each noun (which is often different from genders of your language), but you must also learn to ignore this detail when using nouns with a possessive pronoun in the third person only, and, instead, keep track of the gender of the person possessing the noun like you do in English! 🤯

title: @burkov
clean_title: How Chinese companies catch up in coding models using high signal-to-noise data
summary:
Someone asked how a Chinese company managed to catch up to Codex and Claude Code in coding. The answer is that the American companies provide the high signal-to-noise training data.
The way it works is as follows (all is scripted, no human in the loop):
1. You take a large enough base model and finetune it using a combination of reinforcement learning and supervised finetuning.
2. To get training examples, you ask some LLM to introduce a subtle bug into an existing codebase and provide a test script that would only return True when the bug is fixed.
3. You use Codex/Claude Code to fix the bug. When they do that, you record all LLM inputs and outputs.
4. You use these inputs/outputs for supervised finetuning of your model.
5. You use the test script result (True/False) for reinforcement learning.
Supervised finetuning trains the conversational part of the problem solving. Reinforcement learning trains the actual problem-solving part.
This way, you don't train a weaker student. Verifiable results (True/False) combined with a solution space exploration technique is what eventually makes the student stronger than the teacher.
Coding LLMs is a solved problem and everyone will end up having the same solution.
clean_summary:
Someone asked how a Chinese company managed to catch up to Codex and Claude Code in coding. The answer is that American companies provide high signal-to-noise training data.

The process involves finetuning a large base model with reinforcement learning and supervised finetuning. They generate training examples by asking an LLM to introduce subtle bugs into code and then use Codex or Claude Code to fix them. All inputs and outputs are recorded for supervised finetuning, while the test results guide reinforcement learning. This combination trains both the problem-solving and conversational aspects, making the model stronger than the teacher. The claim is that coding LLMs is a solved problem and everyone will converge on similar solutions.
